en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chueh-wu:

As for those in the world who are called followers of the Pure Land school, the tradition began with Dharma Master Huiyuan of the Jin dynasty. He looked up to embody the Buddha’s compassion and grandly opened the gateway of salvation.

He excavated a pond and planted lotuses, and constructed a hall where he established a vow. At that time, there were eighteen worthy ones and one hundred and twenty-three individuals who had attained the power of mastery;
they contemplated through non-contemplation and were born through non-birth. The Mind-Seal was transmitted in succession, reaching down to the present day without falling into decline.

Among them was the Chan Master Che-wu, the primary successor of the Dharma gate, who from early on possessed both meditative concentration and wisdom, and whose realization accorded with the profound depths.
Wei first realized the essential meaning of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, and subsequently understood the profound purport of the Three Baskets and the Ten Vehicles.
He completely cast aside his former habits and focused single-mindedly on pure karma. With an empty mind and a tranquil spirit, he passed twenty years as if they were a single day.
With a mind free from regression, he was able to fulfill his vow for rebirth in the West.

Thus, one who possesses perfect faith and perfect understanding to benefit sentient beings may take this as proof of Amitābha’s Dharma-realm. His collected works remain extant; reading them, one gains even greater conviction in what the Master taught:
namely, aspiration, faith, practice, the repentance and removal of karmic offenses, and the maturation of roots of goodness—these essentials are indeed...
To be vigilant regarding the arising of the single mind: it spans horizontally throughout the ten directions and extends vertically through the three periods of time;

such is the vastness of the mind. To fear falling into partiality or narrowness and to give rise to great bodhicitta; such is the magnanimity of the mind. Therein, karma is spontaneously induced and transformed into accord with the Way.
The mind is the pivot. It is like casting a clear pearl into turbid water; it is the sowing of melons and beans that yields their respective harvests;

it is the mold that fashions gold into the form of a face. The mind is the source. Regarding the two phrases from the Sūtras—“this mind makes the Buddha” and “this mind is the Buddha”—one must seek their meaning with repeated care and attend to them with utmost earnestness.
Furthermore, it is said: "An inch of time is an inch of life's light. If one wishes for the future...

Among those who study this, by following its swift practice and simplicity amidst the sands of the Ganges, they will quickly pass through the gateway of birth and death and together realize the realm of peace and bliss.
To rescue the multitude of deluded beings and cause them all to ascend to the other shore—how profound is this intention!
Although the Master did not habitually devote his mind to words and letters, he occasionally offered a brief utterance that encompassed the great whole.
There is nothing left out. Its subtle essence is perfectly interfused and unimpeded; it establishes teachings according to the capacities of beings, and its true principle encompasses all.
It is like the *agada* medicine, which cures every ailment; it is like the wish-fulfilling jewel, which satisfies every aspiration—is this not so?

I have privately reflected that while the records of both the doctrinal and Chan schools are as vast as the ocean, and the commentaries on the sutras and annotations on their meanings clarify the Dharma’s intent, yet...
The cultivation of pure karma is the correct path for entering the Way. Aside from the various collections by Longshu Daoyou, there have been few who have spoken of it;

thus, the Master’s words must not be allowed to sink into oblivion. The Master’s eminent disciple Songquan has commissioned the carving of these collections for publication and requested a preface from me.
Since I am one who has delved into the profound and extensive depths of the Master’s writings, I shall elaborate upon them here. This serves as the preface.
The Disciple of the Triple Gem, Cheng’an, respectfully records this preface.
Since the year of Gui-si (1793) of the Qianlong era, I have resided as abbot at Guangtong Temple in the capital, leading the assembly in Zen practice. Among them, there were some from the East...
I spoke in the Western language and recorded it with my pen. Reaching the year of Dingmao (1237), because my past karma was deep and heavy, I encountered many causes for illness.

Consequently, I reflected upon the Five Stopping-Mind Contemplations (*pañca-vinodana*) of the Śāsanā; since sentient beings burdened by many obstacles are treated through the recitation of the Buddha’s name, I focused on this single gateway.
Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and all the other great Bodhisattvas; Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, and all the other great patriarchs;
Zhiyi, Yongming, Chushi, and Lianchi, and all the other great spiritual friends—to all of them I have turned my heart. What person am I, compared to these?

"How could I dare not take refuge? Thereupon, he established a daily practice of reciting the Buddha's name morning and evening, and those who wished to follow his example as practitioners of *dhyāna* were quite numerous.

Consequently, in accordance with the timing and circumstances, and for the sake of his own practice, he eventually ceased formal *samādhi* retreats and focused solely on mindfulness of the Buddha. At that time, those who held him in high esteem within the monastic community saw their reputations tarnished, and a blaze of slander flared up from all sides.
Because I possessed deep faith in the words of the Buddha, I disregarded these criticisms. All the drafts I had accumulated over more than ten years were, in a single moment—
I relegated them to the category of "Cingding" (miscellaneous). Unbeknownst to me, a busybody of a Chan practitioner sifted through the ashes and retrieved several of these fragments;
yet, even so, not one in a hundred remains. Since then, driven by the winds of worldly activity and led astray by empty fame, I have passed through the two monasteries of Juesheng and Zifu.
There have often been those who requested instructions or sought prefaces and colophons for me; pressed by necessity, I could do nothing else.

I responded accordingly. As days turned into years, these writings accumulated into volumes. In the summer of the Wuchen year, the layman Li Fengchun was listening to my lectures at the mountain hermitage;
having attained awakening upon hearing the Dharma, he sought to have them carved into woodblocks. I said, "This must not be done.
Since I have already retired from the world, what need is there for such literary fame? This is the way even worldly recluses speak, yet I have long since set my mind upon the Pure Land."
Furthermore, what words could possibly remain? Since the layman pressed his request without ceasing, I have composed these few lines to show that they were spoken out of sheer necessity.
Written on the third day after the Double Ninth Festival in the ninth month of the Gengwu year of the Jiaqing era, by the practitioner Nü at Zisi.
In the second year of the Fú era, there was a master in the chamber who chanted the *Nianfo* gāthā.
Elder Nùtáng led the assembly in the diligent cultivation of the Dharma-gate of Holding the Name with the utmost sincerity at Guǎngtōngjué.

He resided in two *araṇyas* for many years. This winter of the Yimao year, he again composed one hundred verses each on the doctrinal principles and the fundamental vehicles (*yāna*) to elucidate their essential subtleties, presenting them to the assembly.
Upon hearing them once, those present felt their hearts overflow with joy and their spirits become tranquil, as if they had attained a profound realization.
Thus, he respectfully embodied the Elder’s [Master Xuyun’s] earnest and repeated efforts for the sake of the multitude.

If these were not recorded, they would surely be lost and forgotten over time; therefore, I have committed them to woodblocks and pears, compiling them into several volumes so that like-minded companions may together savor their meaning. Thus it is said.
On the Buddha’s Day of the year of Bingchen, the first year of the Jiaqing era, the disciple Xin Yu,
with head bowed in reverence,
respectfully inscribed this table of contents for the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chewu.

In the universal teachings shown to the assembly, all dharma-gates take the clarification of the mind as their essential; all practice-gates take the purification of the mind as their essential. Thus, it is said:

In clarifying the mind, nothing is as essential as the recitation of the Buddha's name. By recollecting the Buddha and reciting His name, one will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future.

Without relying on expedient means, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind. Is such recitation of the Buddha not the essential method for clarifying the mind? Furthermore, regarding the essential method for purifying the mind, nothing is as effective as the recitation of the Buddha's name.
When a single thought accords with reality, that is one recitation of the Buddha; when every thought accords with reality, that is the constant practice of recitation.

Mind-moment after mind-moment, one recollects the Buddha. Just as a clear pearl cast into turbid water cannot fail to clarify the water, so too the name of the Buddha cast into a distracted mind cannot fail to transform that mind into the state of Buddhahood.
Is such mindfulness of the Buddha not the essential means for purifying the mind?

A single invocation of the Buddha’s name encompasses the essentials of both the gates of awakening and cultivation. To emphasize awakening, faith is inherent within it; to emphasize cultivation, realization is attained.
Within this, faith, understanding, cultivation, and realization encompass all the various vehicles, both Great and Small;
the essentials of all sutras are fully contained therein without exception. Thus, is not the single phrase "Amitābha" the most essential path?

The single thought-moment of our present mind is entirely true yet becomes delusion; entirely delusive yet is itself truth. Throughout the day it remains unchanging, yet throughout the day it accords with conditions.
If one does not accord with the conditions of the Buddha-realm but instead contemplates the realms of the nine destinies, one will contemplate the six mundane paths rather than the three vehicles;
one will contemplate the three miserable paths rather than the human and heavenly realms; and one will contemplate ghosts and animals rather than...

Contemplate the hells. Since all who possess a mind cannot be without thought, and because the essence of the non-thought mind is realized only by the Buddha alone, everyone from the stage of Equal Enlightenment downward possesses thought.
Whenever a single thought arises, one necessarily falls within the ten realms;
there is no thought that exists outside the ten realms, for there is nothing further beyond the ten dharma-realms. Every arising thought constitutes a [single unit].
Regarding the conditions for receiving birth, it is known that once one understands this principle, there has never been anyone who does not practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

If this mind can correspond with the merits of the Dharma-body and the physical body, as well as the sublime names of his myriad virtues, together with impartial great kindness and great compassion—then [rebirth is assured].
To contemplate the Buddha-dharmadhātu is to bring it into correspondence with the bodhicitta and the six pāramitās and myriad practices.
To contemplate the Bodhisattva-dharmadhātu is to bring it into correspondence with the twelve links of dependent origination through the mind of non-self.
To contemplate the Pratyekabuddha-dharmadhātu is to observe the Four Noble Truths through the mind of non-self. Or, to [contemplate] the four...
The eight dhyānas correspond to the dharma-realm of the devas; furthermore, when associated with the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions, one contemplates the dharma-realm of the devas.

If one corresponds with the five precepts, one contemplates the dharma-realm of humans. If one cultivates dharmas such as the precepts and wholesome deeds while harboring a mind of anger, pride, competitiveness, and contention, one falls into the dharma-realm of the asuras.
If, with a lax and soft mind, one contemplates the inferior grade of the ten unwholesome actions, then...

One falls into the realm of animals. Or, with a mind characterized by a mixture of mildness and intensity, corresponding to the medium grade of the ten non-virtues, one falls into the realm of hungry ghosts.
If, however, with a fierce and blazing mind, one corresponds to the superior grade of the ten non-virtues, one immediately falls into the realm of hell.
The ten non-virtues are: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, frivolous speech, harsh speech, divisive speech, covetousness, [malice, and wrong view].

Anger and wrong views are [the opposites]. To act contrary to these constitutes the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*). You should secretly examine for yourself the thoughts that arise during your daily life:
with which realm do they most frequently correspond, and with which realm do they most intensely correspond?
Then, as for where you shall establish your dwelling and sustain your life in future days, there will be no need to ask others.
All realms of experience are solely induced by karma and solely manifested by the mind. At the very place of their manifestation, they are in essence nothing other than the mind itself.
As long as there is a functioning mind, it cannot be without an object. If the realm of the Buddhas does not manifest, then the realms of the nine destinies manifest;

if the realms of the Three Vehicles do not manifest, then the realms of the six classes of ordinary beings manifest; and if the realms of devas, humans, ghosts, and animals do not manifest, then [the realms of hell and the hungry ghosts] manifest.

Regarding the realms of the hells and the realms manifested by the Buddhas and those of the Three Vehicles: although there are differences in their relative excellence, they all essentially consist of the enjoyment of the bliss of the Dharma.

As for the realms manifested by the various devas of the three worlds, they consist solely of the enjoyment of the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the five sensory desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
The realm of the human path is characterized by an intermingling of suffering and pleasure, varying in degree according to one's respective karma.
In the realm of ghosts and beasts, suffering is abundant and joy is meager; as for the hells, there is nothing but the most extreme suffering.

It is like the mountains, rivers, people, and things seen within a person’s dream—all of these manifest in dependence upon the dreaming mind. If the dreaming mind did not exist, the dream objects would certainly not exist;

likewise, if the dream objects did not exist, the dreaming mind would also not exist. Therefore, one knows that there are no objects outside the mind, and no mind outside of objects. This is entirely so.
The object is the mind; the entire mind is the object. If one examines the effect within the cause, one must contemplate the mind;
if one verifies the cause at the site of the effect, one must contemplate the object. Therefore it is said: there has never been a mind without an object, nor an object without a mind.
The effect necessarily arises from the cause, and the cause necessarily produces the effect. If one truly understands this non-duality and oneness of the cause and effect of mind and object—
If one understands this principle yet still does not practice mindfulness of the Buddha to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, I do not believe them.

To truly act for the sake of birth and death, to resolve to attain Bodhicitta, and to uphold the Buddha’s name with deep faith and aspiration—these sixteen characters constitute the great fundamental outline of the Dharma-door of mindfulness of the Buddha.
If the mind that truly seeks to escape birth and death is not aroused, then all other teachings are... [omitted].
All these are shown to be mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Among all the heavy sufferings of the world, none exceeds birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Failing to realize the end of birth and death, one dies and is born again; life follows death, and death follows life. Emerging from one womb and entering another, casting off one skin-bag and taking up another, the suffering is already unbearable;
how much more so when one has not yet escaped the cycle of rebirth, where one cannot avoid falling into the wombs of pigs or dogs.
What wombs will they not bore through? What donkey-skin bags or horse-skin bags will they not take up?

This human body is most difficult to obtain and most easily lost. A single moment’s lapse of mindfulness leads straight into the evil realms. The three paths of suffering are easy to enter but difficult to leave;
the duration in hell is long and the suffering is heavy. Since the time of the Seven Buddhas, one has been nothing more than an ant for eighty thousand [kalpas].
After the kalpa passed, he had still not escaped his pigeon body; his time in the animal realm was already extreme, and his time in the hells of hungry ghosts was twice as long.

Having endured these long kalpas for so long, when will it end? When will there be rest? Ten thousand sufferings burn him simultaneously; there is no refuge and no salvation. Every time I speak of this, my hair stands on end;
every time I bring it to mind, my five viscera feel as if they are being consumed by fire. Therefore, at this very moment, I deeply contemplate birth and death as if I had lost a loved one.
Regarding my parents, [I must act] as if putting out a fire on my head. Now, while I am subject to birth and death, I seek liberation;

yet all sentient beings likewise dwell in birth and death and should all seek liberation. They and I are fundamentally of one essence, and they have all been my parents throughout many lifetimes and will become Buddhas in the future.
If I do not contemplate their universal deliverance but seek only my own benefit, it would be contrary to reason.
If there is deficiency, the mind will not find peace; how much more so if the Great Mind is not aroused?

Then externally one cannot communicate with the Buddhas, internally one cannot accord with one's original nature, above one cannot perfectly fulfill the Buddha-way, and below one cannot extensively benefit all sentient beings.
How can the affection and attachment of beginningless time be liberated? How can the enmity and transgressions of beginningless time be resolved?

The karmic offenses accumulated over kalpas are difficult to repent and eliminate; the roots of goodness accumulated over kalpas are difficult to bring to maturity. Whatever practices one undertakes, many obstacles and adverse conditions arise.
Even if something were accomplished, it would ultimately fall into the partial and the small; therefore, one must give rise to the great bodhicitta in accordance with the nature of reality.
Once the great mind has been aroused, one should cultivate the great practices.
Among all the gates of practice, there is none like profound faith that is most easy to begin, most easy to accomplish, most perfectly secure, and most perfectly sudden and complete.
One should vow to uphold the names of the Buddhas. That which is called "profound faith" is as follows:

the Brahma-like voice and physical marks of Śākyamuni Tathāgata are certainly free from deceptive speech; the great compassionate heart of Amitābha World-Honored One is certainly free from empty vows.

Furthermore, by means of the cause of reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth, one will inevitably realize the fruit of beholding the Buddha and attaining rebirth, just as planting melons results in melons and planting beans results in beans.
An echo must respond to a sound; a shadow must follow a form. Causes are never discarded in vain, and effects are never obtained without reason.

This is something one can believe with confidence even without waiting to ask a Buddha. How much more so for the nature of mind within our own present single thought: it is entirely true yet becomes delusory, entirely delusory yet is itself true.
Throughout the day it follows conditions, yet throughout the day it remains unchanging. It extends horizontally and exhausts the vertical; in its very substance, it is without [defilement].
Externally, the Pure Land of Amitābha is entirely contained within it. Since I possess the Buddha-mind, I contemplate the Buddha who is inherent within my mind;
how could the Buddha inherent within my mind not respond to the Buddha-mind possessed by me?
The *Wangsheng zhuan* (Biographies of Rebirth) records the auspicious signs at the time of death, arranged in orderly rows; how could these deceive us?

Once one has gained such faith, the longing for rebirth becomes intensely personal. Viewing the suffering of this Sahā world through the lens of the bliss of that land, one’s revulsion and desire for detachment deepen as if fleeing from a latrine pit or escaping from a prison.
Conversely, viewing the bliss of that land from afar through the lens of the suffering of this Sahā world, one feels profound joy.
Exert yourself with earnestness. It is like returning to one’s hometown; it is like rushing toward a place of treasure.

In short, it is like a thirsty person longing for a drink, like a hungry person longing for food, like one suffering from illness longing for excellent medicine, like an infant longing for its compassionate mother, like one fleeing an enemy pursued by a brandished sword, or like one fallen into water or fire urgently seeking rescue. If you can indeed be so earnest, then all [obstacles]...
External conditions and circumstances shall be unable to lead one astray. Thereafter, with this mind of faith and aspiration, one should uphold the Name.
Each single utterance is a seed of the Lotus of the Nine; each single recitation is the direct cause for rebirth in the Pure Land.

One must ensure that the mind continues uninterrupted from moment to moment, without deviation. One must be exclusively focused and diligent, without distraction or interval. As time passes, one’s resolve shall become ever firmer. Thus it turns...
Sustain this through repeated practice for a long, long time until it naturally forms a continuous whole, and you will enter the state of single-mindedness without distraction.
If this is truly so, yet one does not attain rebirth, then Śākyamuni Tathāgata would be a speaker of falsehood and Amitābha Bhagavat would have made a vain vow.
Could such a principle possibly exist?

The two phrases from the *Contemplation Sūtra*, "The mind creates the Buddha" and "The mind is the Buddha," are even more direct and incisive when compared to the Chan School’s "Directly pointing to the human mind, seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha.
Why is this? It is because seeing one's nature is difficult while creating the Buddha is easy. What is meant by "seeing one's nature"?
To see one's nature, one must transcend the mind, intellect, and consciousness until the spiritual radiance suddenly bursts forth; therefore, it is difficult. Why? Because...
To become a Buddha means to hold the name of the Buddha and to contemplate the Buddha’s primary and secondary marks; thus, one becomes a Buddha. Therefore, it is easy. As the Sūtra says:
"When you all bring the Buddha to mind, this very mind is the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.

Is this not to become a Buddha simply by recollecting the Buddha through thought? Now, becoming a Buddha is the state of Buddhahood; in principle, there is no duality between them. Yet, as for what is seen...

The disparity between the ease and difficulty of attaining Buddhahood through one's nature is so vast; is it not therefore the case that, compared to Zen meditation (*chán*), the practice of Buddha-recollection (*niàn fó*) is far more direct and decisive?
One is the word of the Patriarchs, and the other is the word of the Buddha—what is heavy and what is light?
What is to be adopted and what is to be discarded? Students should simply cast aside all old habits, empty their minds, and level their breaths, then try to savor this for a moment.
Examine this; you will surely nod in agreement that this statement is not erroneous.
When Shishuang passed away, the assembly appointed the Head Seat Tai to succeed him as abbot. At that time, Jiufeng Qian served as his attendant.
He then said, "If you are to succeed as abbot, you must clarify the meaning of the former master. Taiyu asked, "What meaning did the former master have?
I do not understand it. Qian said, "The former master constantly taught people to 'rest,' to 'cease,' and to 'go into a state of cold stillness.'"
"Leaving the ancient temple incense burner; going like a single white silk ribbon; going with ten thousand years in a single thought.
As for the rest, I do not ask. What is 'going like a single white silk ribbon'? Tai said, "This merely clarifies matters on the side of 'one color' (monochromatic unity).

Qian said, "It turns out I have not yet understood the late Master’s meaning. Tai said, "Bring some incense. When the incense smoke has completely vanished, if I am unable to go [with it], then you may speak."
He did not grasp the meaning of his former teacher. His attendants immediately prepared incense; before the smoke had even faded, Tai passed away.
Qian patted his back and said, "To sit and die or stand and pass away is not impossible, yet you have not even dreamed of your former teacher’s meaning.
When Cao Shan was seated upon the dais, the Paper-Clothing Ascetic passed by below the hall. Shan asked, "Could that be the Paper-Clothing Ascetic?"
Zhaozhou said, "I dare not. Mount Yunmen asked, "What is the matter beneath the paper robe? Zhaozhou said, "Once the single fur cloak is hung upon the body, all phenomena are entirely as they are.
Yunmen asked, "What is the function beneath the paper robe? Zhaozhou said, "Yes," and then he passed away.

Mount said, "You only understand going in this way; you do not understand coming in this way. Daoyi again opened his eyes and asked, "What is it like when the one spiritual true nature does not rely on a womb?
Mount said, "That is not yet marvelous. As for 'passing away while sitting' or 'dying while standing,' [it is not so]."
Not yet having clarified the Great Dharma, one certainly has not finished with the matter. Nevertheless, the depth of such cultivation and effort is by no means easy.

If you can truly turn this energy toward single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking birth in the Pure Land, you will surely attain stable rebirth in the highest grade of the highest level;
how could you ever again be subject to others’ scrutiny? As when Zhiyi asked, "What is the wondrous? and Tiantai Shan replied:

He said, "Not borrowed, not borrowed. He then respectfully took leave of his robes and passed away. Alas! Rather than borrowing the foul and filthy womb without having borrowed it, how much better is it to borrow the fragrant and pure lotus flower without having borrowed it?
To speak merely of the foulness of the womb versus the fragrance and purity of the lotus, the difference between them is already vast and profound.

How much more so when one emerges from the womb and crosses over the barrier of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), where assuming mastery is exceedingly difficult—especially for one who dwells within the lotus.

The womb is but a single layer, yet the superior conditions for rebirth are fully met; thus, the difference between a day and an eon is as vast as the gap between heaven and earth, beyond all analogy.
It is no wonder that the Great Master Yongming said: "With Chan but no Pure Land, nine out of ten go astray;
with Chan and the Pure Land, ten thousand who practice, ten thousand depart. These are words of truth, words of reality. O Great Compassionate One!
These words, spoken with tears of compassion from the depths of one’s entrails, are for scholars to take to heart and not neglect.
At the very beginning, when delusion arises from the truth, it is called "a single thought of deluded movement.

At the final stage, when returning from delusion to the truth, it is called "a single thought of resonance. Between the arising of delusion and the return to truth, what other dharma could there possibly be that exists apart from this?

Is this not a single thought-moment? Therefore, when a single thought awakens and follows pure conditions, it is the Buddha-dharmadhātu; when it is deluded and follows defiled conditions, it is the nine realms of existence.
The empty space of the ten directions is this single thought-moment in its state of confusion and obscurity; all lands are this single thought-moment in its state of clarity and concentration.

The primary retribution of the four modes of birth is this single thought-moment of the union and separation of feeling and perception; the secondary retribution of the four elements is this single thought-moment.
This single thought—its movement and stillness, its opposition and compliance—manifests all phenomena solely by depending upon this thought. Apart from this thought, no phenomenon can be found.
Tracing back to its origin, this single thought is fundamentally the Dharma-realm; it arises from conditions, yet those conditions have no inherent nature of their own.

The entire dharma-realm is thus horizontally pervasive throughout the ten directions and vertically exhaustive across the three periods of time. It is free from faults and transcends all that is non-virtuous; it is inconceivable.
By its very nature, it possesses this majestic spiritual power; by its very nature, it possesses this functional efficacy.

Now, with this mindfulness, one recollects Amitābha Buddha of the West, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. At the very moment of such recollection, the environment and the inhabitants of the West—both the physical realm and the enlightened beings—[manifest].
Within my mind, this very mind of mine already dwells within the Western Land’s environment and its inhabitants.
It is like two mirrors reflecting each other’s light, mutually containing and illuminating one another; this is the aspect of horizontal pervasiveness throughout the ten directions.

If we consider it in terms of vertical penetration through the three periods of time, then the moment of reciting the Buddha’s name is the moment of seeing the Buddha, and it is also the moment of attaining Buddhahood. The moment of seeking rebirth is the moment of being reborn there. Furthermore—

At the very moment of delivering sentient beings, the three periods of time are simultaneous; there is no longer any sequence of before or after. Like the light of pearls in Indra’s net, it is difficult to equate with the entirety [of reality].
The events of the "Dream of the Southern Branch" roughly resemble one class of this phenomenon. This principle is most difficult to awaken to, yet easiest to believe.

If one can simply accept it directly and immediately, one will ultimately enjoy its full benefit throughout one's entire being. This may be called the completion of one's studies and the fulfillment of what was to be done.
If you are still unable to do so, you should simply observe things as they are and make use of them according to your capacity.
The mind can create karma; the mind can transform karma. Karma is created by the mind; karma follows the mind.
If the mind cannot transform karma, it is bound by karma; if karma does not follow the mind, it can bind the mind. Why is it that the mind can transform karma?
When the mind merges with the Way and the mind merges with the Buddha, one is then able to transform karma. How can karma bind the mind?
The mind relies upon habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and undergoes experiences through their spontaneous operation; this is what constitutes being bound by karma.

All present environments and all future retributions are solely induced by karma and are solely manifestations of the mind. Because they are solely induced by karma, the preceding objects and the subsequent retributions [arise].
All things possess a fixed nature because karma is able to bind the mind, and because all that appears is manifested solely by the mind.
Conversely, the circumstances of one's environment and retributions lack any fixed nature because the mind is able to transform karma.

If, at the very moment when karma is binding the mind and the circumstances of one's environment and retribution are fixed, a person suddenly gives rise to a vast and great mind and practices the authentic path, their mind will merge with the Buddha. Their mind...
When one is in accord with the Way, the mind can transform karma; thus, when a prior object presents itself as retribution, it is fixed yet not fixed.

Furthermore, when the mind can transform karma and the prior object presenting itself as retribution is not yet fixed, if the great mind suddenly regresses and true practice suffers a deficiency, then karma can bind the mind;
consequently, the prior object presenting itself as retribution becomes fixed despite being unfixed. However, this karma was created in the past. This...

Then there is nothing that can be done. Fortunately, whether or not one arouses the mind [of enlightenment] depends upon one’s own capacity; the creation and transformation of karma do not depend on others.

If we, right now, arouse the mind to recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss—whether by contemplating the environment and its inhabitants or by holding the Name—if our mindfulness continues in uninterrupted succession until it reaches its ultimate point, then the mind will merge with the Buddha. Upon merging...

Furthermore, through unification—reaching the ultimate of such unification—the mind is able to transform karma, so that the present realm of Saṃsāra is transformed into Sukhāvatī, and the retribution of the womb or the hells is transformed into the calyx of a lotus;
one thus becomes a person of sovereign mastery in the Land of Bliss.
Yet, at such a time, if the mind should by chance lose its illumination or suddenly give rise to regret and retreat, failing to remain in union with the Buddha, then...
Karma can bind the mind, yet the objects before us continue to appear as retributions; they remain, as ever, the suffering sentient beings of this Sahā world.
Therefore, those among us who are resolved to transcend [suffering] and seek rebirth in the Pure Land should not fail to be stirred with earnest caution.
How truly resolute was his resolve!
Within the gateway of the Pure Land, the vow is paramount. For all who possess a vow, it shall ultimately be fulfilled.

Take, for example, Udraka Rāmaputra, who practiced the concentration on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by the waterside and beneath the forest trees; every time he was about to achieve that meditative state, he was repeatedly interrupted by fish and birds.
Startled, he made an evil vow, saying: "In a future life, I shall become a flying cat. Entering the forest, I will eat birds; entering the water, I will eat fish.

Later, having perfected the meditative concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), he was reborn in the heavens with a lifespan of eighty thousand great kalpas. When his celestial retribution was exhausted, [he fell].
He consequently fell into the form of a flying cat (*fēilí*), entering forests and waters to feed on fish and birds;

this was an evil vow that contradicted his nature, yet it still possessed great power and efficacy. If even such a thing can be fulfilled after eighty thousand *kalpas*, how much more so a virtuous vow made in accordance with one's true nature?
The *Shenseng zhuan* records a monk who, before a stone Buddha, playfully made a vow, saying: "If in this life my cycle of birth and death is not brought to an end, I vow—"
"In my future life, may I become a powerful and majestic minister. Later, he indeed became a great general; this was the vow he made during that play.

If even such a vow was ultimately fulfilled, how much more so must a vow made with utmost sincerity? Furthermore, there was another monk who was widely learned in the sutras and śāstras, yet wherever he went, he met with no success.
He sighed and lamented deeply, whereupon a fellow monk beside him said: "In your study of the Buddha-dharma, have you not heard alone—"
"Before attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, one must first establish karmic connections with people. Although you are well-versed in the Buddha-dharma, what can you do if you lack such connections?
The monk asked, "Will I pass away right here? A nearby monk said, "I shall act on your behalf. He asked what the monk possessed;
the monk replied, "Nothing else, only a single bolt of cloth remaining. [The other monk] said, "This will suffice," and subsequently exchanged it for its value and established [the connection].
He purchased food and led the monk to a deep forest where birds and insects were very numerous.
He placed the food on the ground and further instructed him to make a vow, saying: "Twenty years from now, you may then begin to teach the Dharma.
The monk followed these instructions, and only after twenty years did he finally begin to teach the Dharma. Those who received his transformation numbered many; indeed, they were all...
Even birds and insects that consume his food [are saved]. Such is the inconceivable power of this vow-force (*praṇidhāna-bala*).

If he can even use the vows of others to gather those insects and birds, liberating them from their animal states and causing them to enter the human realm, how could he not be able to save himself through his own vows?
It was by means of the forty-eight vows that the Buddha attained Buddhahood; the vows I have now made are precisely...
This accords with the Buddha’s vow to gather in and sustain all living beings; thus, by simply making this vow, one may attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
How much more so when the Buddha possesses inconceivable great kindness and great compassion! Like a polished white jade, he makes no distinction between those who consume wine and meat and others.

Later, as I read the *Biographies of Those Who Attained Rebirth*, I felt a deep sense of conviction at every biography I encountered. Consequently, I ceased eating food and devoted myself to the recitation of the Buddha's name for seven days, until I was moved by the manifestation of the Buddha.
The Buddha consoled him, saying, "Your remaining lifespan is still ten years. You should diligently practice mindfulness of the Buddha; I shall come to receive you after ten years.
Fakuo said, "The Sahā world is turbid and evil, making it easy to lose right mindfulness. I pray that I may be born early in the Pure Land to serve the various sages.
The Buddha said, "Since your resolve is such as this, I shall come to receive you in three days' time. After three days, he indeed attained rebirth there.

There was also Chan Master Huaiyu, who cultivated the Pure Land practices with great diligence. One day, he saw Buddhas and Bodhisattvas filling the void of space, and a person carrying a silver platform entered.
Huaiyu thought to himself, "Throughout my life I have been diligent in practice, my aspiration being for the Golden Platform.
Why is it now otherwise? Thereupon, the silver platform vanished. Huaiyu redoubled his efforts in cultivation. Twenty-one days later, he again beheld the Buddha.
Bodhisattvas filled the void. He who had previously borne the silver terrace arrived instead with a golden terrace, and Yu then departed in serene stillness.
Liu Yimin relied upon Donglin to form a society for the recitation of the Buddha's name. One day, while he was contemplating the Buddha, he saw the Buddha manifest his body.
Liu thought, "How can I obtain the Tathāgata’s hand to stroke my head? The Buddha immediately stroked his head with his hand.
He further thought, "How wonderful it would be if the Tathāgata’s robe were to cover my body! The Buddha immediately covered his body with His robe. Alas!
The Buddha’s reach toward sentient beings is nowhere limited; He can truly be called a parent of great compassion.

If one desires to be reborn quickly, He causes them to be reborn quickly. If one desires a golden platform, He changes it into a golden platform. If one desires His hand to touch one's head, He touches one's head.
If one desires clothing to cover the body, it shall immediately cover the body. Since the Buddha is compassionate toward all sentient beings, how could he alone not be compassionate toward me?
Since the Buddha fulfills the vows of all sentient beings, how could he alone not fulfill my vow?
Great compassion makes no distinctions; how could such a thing be possible? Therefore, if one can truly make a vow, faith will reside therein.
Within this, once faith and aspiration are genuine, practice will arise spontaneously without being sought.
Therefore, the three types of provisions—faith, aspiration, and practice—are fully encompassed by the single character "aspiration" (yuan).
Among all things in the world, there is nothing more precious than the spirit; among all things in the world, there is nothing more worthy of being cherished than time.
A single thought of purity is the dependent origination of the Buddha-realm; a single thought of defilement is the cause for birth within the nine realms.
Every movement of a single thought is the seed of the ten realms—how can one not cherish this? This day has already passed, and life likewise diminishes accordingly.
A single inch of time is a single inch of the light of life; how can one not cherish it? If you know that the spirit is something precious, do not squander it.
Instead, maintain the recitation of the Buddha’s name in every thought-moment so that your time is not spent in vain, and cultivate pure karma at every instant.
Should you set aside the Buddha’s name to practice other noble deeds of the Three Vehicles, this too is a waste of effort.

This spirit is like a crossbow capable of lifting a thousand *jin* being released for the sake of a mere field mouse; how much more so when it concerns the hands that create the karma of birth and death within the six realms of existence?
If one were to set aside the practice of pure karma (*śuddha-karma*) to instead pursue the provisional vehicles and their minor fruits, this too would be a vain squandering of one's time.
It is as if one were trading a wish-fulfilling jewel for a single garment or a single meal; how much more so when seeking the tainted fruits of the human and celestial realms?

If you thus hold [the practice] in high esteem and cherish it with such care, your mind will become focused and the Buddha will be easily invoked. Your conduct will be diligent and your karma easily refined.
Thus, you shall truly attain birth in the Pure Land, personally behold Amitābha, receive his instructions at that time, and face-to-face receive his compassionate grace.
Yin: Wondrously awakening to one’s own mind and profoundly realizing the Dharma-realm, one extends a single thought-moment into a long kalpa and contracts a long kalpa into a single thought-moment.
With the perfect fusion of thought-moments and kalpas, one attains great mastery. Is this not the fruition of having personally consumed that which was cherished and treasured?

Generally, one realizes the Way (*darśanamārga*) before cultivating it (*bhāvanāmārga*), and cultivates it before realizing its fruit (*adhigamamārga*). This is the common path of the thousand sages and an immutable doctrine established throughout the ages.
Yet, how easy is it to speak of realizing the Way? If one follows the Scriptural Vehicle (*śāstrayāna*), one must first develop a vast and perfect understanding;
if one follows the School of the Gate (*mukhayāna*), one must directly penetrate the heavy barriers. Only then can one discuss the cultivation of the Way; otherwise, it is not so.
Those who practice blindly and train recklessly will inevitably collide with walls and strike against barriers, falling into pits and ravines.
Only the single gateway of the Pure Land is not thus. To the west, beyond a hundred trillion Buddha-lands, there is a world named Sukhāvatī.
In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who currently dwells and expounds the Dharma. Simply by making a vow and upholding His name, one immediately—
One will attain rebirth there. This is a realm personally known and personally seen by the Buddha’s own heart and eye;

it is not something that can be known or seen by the worthy ones and sages of the three vehicles. One should simply have deep faith in the Buddha’s words and, relying upon them, make vows and hold the Name.
This means that one takes the Buddha’s knowledge and vision as one's own knowledge and vision; there is no need to seek a separate gate of enlightenment.

Regarding the cultivation of the Way through other gates, one must necessarily awaken first and then practice according to the Dharma: by gathering the mind, one achieves meditative concentration (*samādhi*); based on concentration, wisdom (*prajñā*) arises; and based on wisdom, delusions are severed.
The wisdom that arises has degrees of superiority and inferiority, and the delusions that are severed have varying depths. Only after this can one discuss whether there is regression.

Regarding non-retrogression: it is only within this gateway of the Pure Land that by relying solely on the mind of faith and aspiration and single-mindedly upholding the Name until one reaches the state of "one-pointedness without distraction," the pure karma is fully perfected. After death, rebirth in the Pure Land is certain;

once rebirth is attained, one shall never again fall back. Furthermore, regarding the cultivation of the Way through other gateways, one must first repent for one's current karma. If [this] current karma...
If one does not repent, it will immediately obstruct the Path, leaving no way to advance in cultivation. Those who practice the Pure Land method are reborn while still carrying their karmic burdens;

they do not need to repent for their karma, because a single utterance of the Buddha’s name with a sincere mind can extinguish the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.

Furthermore, in other gateways to the Path, one must sever the afflictions (*kleśa*); if even a fraction of the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* and *bhava-rāga*) remains unextinguished...
If these are not exhausted, then birth-and-death in segmented portions will not be ended, and one will be unable to escape the Land of Common Residence.
Only by cultivating pure karma can one emerge horizontally from the triple world; without severing the afflictions, one moves from this Land of Common Residence to that Land of Common Residence.
Once born in that land, the very roots of birth-and-death are forever severed. Having been born in that land, one constantly sees the Buddha at all times.
At that time, one hears the Dharma; clothing, food, and dwelling appear spontaneously. Water birds and forest trees all preach the Dharma.

Dwelling within that land, one horizontally perceives the three superior pure lands. One gathers with all the supreme virtuous ones in a single place, perfectly realizing the three types of non-retrogression, and in a single lifetime, one fills the rank of a Buddha.
Thus, the gate of the Pure Land is the very first means for seeking awakening.
This gate does not require the subsequent arousal of wisdom, nor the confession of karma, nor the severing of afflictions;
it is the ultimate in brevity and essentiality, the ultimate in directness and swiftness. When one realizes and enters it, it is the ultimate in vastness and the ultimate in finality.
Students should contemplate and savor this with a refined mind, examining it in detail; do not, out of temporary pride, lose sight of this most excellent and supreme benefit.
There was a destitute man who, gazing from afar, saw a string of coins. He approached and picked them up, only to find they were a snake. He stood there staring in astonishment.
Then another person arrived, took the string of coins, and departed. Although the money was not a snake, the snake had appeared.
These are manifested solely by karma and manifested solely by the mind. The snake upon the coin is certainly a manifestation of the mind induced by karma;
yet, is the coin upon the snake not likewise a manifestation of the mind induced by karma? The snake upon the coin is the deluded vision of an individual’s distinct karma (*bhedakarma*);
the coin upon the snake is the deluded vision of the common lot (*sabhāgatā*) of many people. This is the delusion of a single person...
The delusion of seeing [a snake] is easy to recognize; the deluded perceptions of many people are difficult to recognize.

By using what is easy to recognize as a model for what is difficult to recognize, even that which is difficult to recognize becomes easy to recognize. Thus, the snake is indeed a snake, and the coin is also a snake. Extending this reasoning further:

Internally, the sense organs and the body; externally, the objective realms—from one direction to the ten directions, and including the four great continents and the trichiliocosm—all are but snakes upon this coin. Once the snake of "mind-only" appears, it can bite;
once the coin of "mind-only" appears, one gains enjoyment. This does not mean that [the world] is simply mind-only.
There are no external objects. Furthermore, the defiled suffering of this Sahā world and the pure bliss of Sukhāvatī both manifest solely from the mind.
When the defiled suffering of the mind manifests, one undergoes great oppression; when the pure bliss of the mind manifests, one attains great enjoyment.
Since both defiled suffering and pure bliss manifest solely from the mind, why not abandon the defiled suffering of the mind? By means of...
One grasps at the purity and bliss of the mind-only, yet for long kalpas one willingly undergoes the intense searing of the eight sufferings.
At the critical juncture of birth and death for us humans, there are only two forces: first, the manifold tendencies of the mind, which cause one to fall toward whatever is most weighty.
This is the power of the mind (*citta-bala*). Second, it is like a person who owes a debt; the stronger creditor drags them forward first. This is the power of karma (*karma-bala*).

The power of karma is greatest, yet the power of the mind is even greater. Because karma has no self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and depends entirely upon the mind, the mind can create karma and the mind can transform karma.
Therefore, while the power of karma is merely strong, the power of the mind alone is weighty; only when combined with a heavy mind can it drag one toward rebirth. If, by means of a heavy mind...
By thus cultivating pure karma, that pure karma becomes powerful; when the mind is focused and karma is strong, one will head exclusively toward the Western Quarter.
Consequently, when the time comes for the end of life and the exhaustion of the lifespan, one will certainly go to the Western Quarter and not be born in any other place.
It is like a large tree or a great wall that habitually leans toward the west; if they were to fall one day, they would certainly not fall in any other direction. What constitutes a "heavy mind"? We—
In cultivating pure karma, faith is valued for its depth and aspiration for its urgency.
Because faith is deep and aspiration is urgent, no heterodox teachings can shake or delude one, and no objective conditions can lead one astray. When one is correctly cultivating pure karma:
Should Master Dharma suddenly appear before you, he will say: "I possess the Chan that directly points to the human mind for the realization of Buddhahood.
You need only set aside your recitation of the Buddha's name, and I shall transmit this Chan to you. At that time, you should simply pay obeisance to the Patriarch and say:
"I have already received the Dharma-gate of reciting the Buddha's name from Śākyamuni Tathāgata, and I have made a vow to uphold it."
"I shall not change for the rest of my life. Although the Patriarch possesses a profound and wondrous path of Chan, I dare not violate my original vow.
Even if Śākyamuni Tathāgata were to suddenly manifest before me and say: 'When I previously taught the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha, it was merely a temporary expedient.
Now there is a more sublime Dharma-gate that surpasses that one; you should [practice this instead],' I would still..."
"Setting aside the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, I shall instead expound for you the Supreme Dharma. Furthermore, you should simply bow your head before the Buddha and declare:
'I have previously received from the World-Honored One the Dharma-gate of Pure Practice; as long as I draw one more breath, I vow never to alter it.
Although the Tathāgata possesses the Supreme Dharma, I dare not contravene my original vow. Even if the Buddhas and Patriarchs were to manifest in person, [one would still not change]."
If one can change even what one holds dear, how much more so the false and delusive teachings of Māra and the non-Buddhists—how could they possibly shake one’s faith?

To be able to believe in this way is to possess what may be called a profound faith. Even if a glowing iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of one’s head, one would not retreat from the vow for rebirth in that land because of such suffering;
nor would one be moved by the appearance of the sublime five desires of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).

One might lose the aspiration for rebirth due to such worldly pleasures; yet, even when faced with the ultimate extremes of adversity and favor, one does not alter this vow—how much less could the minor circumstances of the mundane world turn it away?
To be able to make such a vow is to have a vow that may be called earnest.
When faith is deep and the vow is earnest, this is what is meant by a "resolute mind. Cultivating pure karma with such a mind ensures that the pure karma will necessarily be powerful.

Because it is weighty, it is easily purified; because its karma is powerful, it is easily matured. If the pure karma of Sukhāvatī has matured, then the defiled conditions of Saṃsāra will come to an end.
Once the defiled conditions have truly ended, then at the time of death, even if one wishes for the realms of saṃsāra to reappear before one’s eyes, they cannot do so.
Once the pure karma has truly matured, then at the time of death, even if one wishes to remain in [this world]...
The Pure Land of Amitābha does not appear before one, nor can it be attained by mere chance; however, this faith and aspiration must be cultivated through long-standing practice.

If one maintains them consistently, one will naturally avoid straying onto divergent paths at the critical moment. For example, when an ancient master was about to pass away, celestial youths from the six heavens of the desire realm came in succession to invite him, yet he would not go.
He focused his mind solely on awaiting the Buddha; only after the Buddha appeared did he say, "The Buddha has come!"
He then joined his palms and passed away. Now, when one is about to reach the end of life, the four elements disintegrate; what time is this?

When the youths of the six heavens of desire arrive in succession to lead one away; what realm is this? If one’s habitual faith and aspiration have not reached a state of ten-fold firmness, how could one possibly maintain mastery over oneself at such a time, in the face of such a realm?
As the ancient masters truly said: [Insert relevant verse here] Thus it may be said.
This is the banner held by those who have cultivated the practice of Pure Land for a thousand ages.
A Chan practitioner asked: "All phenomena are entirely like dreams; the Sahā world is certainly a dream, and the Land of Ultimate Bliss is likewise a dream.
Since both are equally one dream, what benefit is there in practicing? I replied: "Not so. Prior to the seventh stage [of the Bodhisattva path]..."
One cultivates the Way within a dream; ignorance is a great dream, wherein even those who have attained equal enlightenment still sleep. Only the Buddha alone is truly called the Great Awakened One.
While the eyes of the dream have not yet opened, suffering and pleasure are vividly present.

Rather than experiencing the extreme sufferings of the Sahā world within a dream, why not experience the wondrous bliss of Sukhāvatī within a dream? Moreover, the dream of the Sahā world is a dream within a dream—a dream upon a dream.

The former dream is that of one who is increasingly mired in delusion; the dream of the Pure Land is that which proceeds from dreaming toward awakening, and through awakening upon awakening, gradually reaches Great Awakening.
Although the dreams are the same, the nature of those who dream is never the same.
How can they be discussed in general terms?

The ocean of the Buddha-dharma is entered through faith; among its various gates, that of the Pure Land is especially essential because the practice of reciting the Name is the profound sphere of action of all Buddhas, which can be understood only in part by Bodhisattvas bound to one more birth.

As for all other worthy sages and saints, they can only be followed and believed; they are not within the scope of what one's own intellectual capacity can know, let alone the inferior ordinary person.
Nevertheless, among the eleven wholesome dharmas, faith occupies the first place; prior to the stage of faith, there is no further wholesome dharma.
Among the fifty-five stages, faith is the beginning; prior to the stage of faith, there is no distinct stage of sainthood. Therefore—
The Bodhisattva composed the *Awakening of Faith*, and the Patriarch [Huineng] wrote the *Inscription on Faith*. They took the single dharma of faith as the essential gateway for entering the Way.
Formerly, Wang Zhonghui asked Yang Wuweishi, "How can one practice the recitation of the Buddha's name so that it remains uninterrupted?
Yang replied, "Once you have attained faith, do not doubt again. Wang departed with joy. Not long after, Yang...
Dong Zhonghui sent word to express his gratitude, saying that because he had received your instructions, he had gained great benefit and had already been reborn in the Pure Land.
Later, Yang met Zhonghui’s son and inquired about the circumstances and the specific time of his father’s departure.
On the very day Zhengyang obtained this dream, one sighs: "How great indeed is the significance of the timing!
The Bhikṣu Dharmakara, in the presence of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, made forty-eight great vows that accord with the nature of reality.
In accordance with these vows, he practiced the Great Deeds for immeasurable and long kalpas until, his causes being perfected and his fruits fulfilled, he attained Buddhahood of his own accord.

The Buddha’s Dharma-treasury was renamed Amitābha, and his world was renamed Sukhāvatī. That Amitābha is called Amitābha is because he has profoundly realized that the self-nature of mind alone is such.
Yet, is this Amitābha and Sukhāvatī not the Amitābha of self-nature and the Sukhāvatī of the mind-only?
For this nature of mind is the equal possession of both sentient beings and Buddhas; it does not belong exclusively to one side.
The Buddha, likewise, does not belong exclusively to sentient beings. If one regards the mind as belonging to Amitābha, then sentient beings are the sentient beings within Amitābha’s mind;
if one regards the mind as belonging to sentient beings, then Amitābha is the Amitābha within the minds of sentient beings.
Since sentient beings are the sentient beings within Amitābha’s mind, and Amitābha is the Amitābha within the minds of sentient beings, how could it be that [sentient beings] do not [attain him]?
If Amitābha is within the mind, should not sentient beings likewise be within the mind of Amitābha?

It is simply that the Buddha has awakened to this mind, like a person who has woken from sleep, whereas sentient beings are deluded regarding this mind, like people in a dream. Apart from the person who has woken, there is no separate person in the dream;
how could there be a person who has woken apart from the person in the dream? It is merely a matter of being in a dream.
A person should not consider themselves to be real, nor should they seek a person of the waking state apart from the person within the dream.
One should simply constantly remember the person of the waking state. By remembering again and again, one will see the great dream gradually awaken and the eyes of the dream open wide;
the very person who is able to remember within the dream is precisely the person of the waking state who is being remembered. And...
One who is awake is not the same as one in a dream. Those within a dream are many; those who are awake are but one.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions share a single Dharma-body; they are of one mind and one wisdom, and their powers and fearlessnesses are likewise the same.
This is the principle of being both one and many, both eternally identical and eternally distinct—the naturally wondrous nature of phenomena. Such is the intent of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection).
The general outline is as follows:
"When born, one is certainly born; when departing, one truly does not depart. These two phrases—the first speaks of phenomena (*dharma*), and the second speaks of principle (*li*).
Phenomena (*shi*) are phenomena that are identical with principle (*li*); this means that arising is non-arising, rather than taking mere arising as arising.
Principle is principle that is identical with phenomena; this means that non-going is going, rather than taking mere non-going as non-going.
If one views these two phrases as a single phrase, then phenomena and principle are perfectly interfused—what is called "the dual excellence when united. If [one views] the two phrases...
If you view these as two separate phrases, then phenomena and principle will be split apart; this is what is meant by "separating them results in injury to both.
If, however, these two phrases are not combined into one, they should instead be expanded from these two into four:

namely, "if born, certainly born; yet born without being born"; "if departed, truly not departed; yet not departed while departing. Although these constitute four phrases, their meaning remains [as one].
There is no increase; taken together as a single phrase, its meaning likewise does not decrease. It is simply that the principle and the phenomenon are perfectly interfused.
Rather than clinging to the principle that "though one goes, in reality one does not go," it is better to cling to the fact that "if there is birth, there is certainly birth. Why?

Because while clinging to phenomena may obscure the principle, it still does not negate the merit of entering the stages of practice. However, if one clings to the principle and abandons phenomena, then [the practice] ceases to exist.
This avoids the reproach of falling into emptiness, for phenomena possess the function of accompanying principle, and principle lacks the capacity to exist independently.
To take arising as arising is to fall into the view of eternalism; to take non-departure as non-departure is to fall into the view of nihilism.
Although eternalism and nihilism are equally false views, the faults of nihilism are more profound and grave; therefore, it is better to cling to phenomena than [to cling to principle].
This is acceptable; however, it is not as excellent as the two phrases "perfectly interfusing" (*yuánhuì*).

Our present single thought-moment is dependently originated and devoid of self-nature (*anātman*); being devoid of self-nature yet dependently originated, if it does not give rise to the Buddha-realm, it gives rise to the nine realms.

If we consider it from the perspective of dependent origination being devoid of self-nature, then the arising of Buddhas and [sentient beings] are equal within the single emptiness. If we consider it from the perspective of [self-nature] being devoid...
Upon birth, the superiority and inferiority of the ten realms differ vastly. King Ajita, at the moment of his death, was fanning his face with a whisk held by a fly-sweeper;
yet due to a single thought of anger, he fell into the form of a venomous snake. A certain woman, while crossing a river, lost her grip and her child fell into the water;
as she reached out to retrieve him, she drowned along with him. However, because of her compassionate heart, she attained rebirth in the heavens. Indeed, a single...

When one contemplates loving-kindness, anger subsides; when one contemplates heaven, the animal realm is left behind. Thus, regarding this single thought that arises at the moment of death, how can one not be cautious?
If one uses this mind to contemplate Amitābha and seeks rebirth in the Pure Land, will one not surely see the Buddha and attain rebirth?
However, this single thought cannot be achieved through mere luck; it must be maintained with sincerity and cultivated through long-standing practice. This is so.

Therefore, when we recite this single phrase of Amitābha—reciting it with a thousand thoughts and ten thousand thoughts, even throughout our entire lives and years—it is none other than for the sake of making this one thought thoroughly matured.
Once this one thought is truly matured, at the time of death there will be only this one thought and no other.
As the Great Master Zhiyi said: "The mind in meditative concentration at the moment of death..."
This is precisely the mind that seeks rebirth in the Pure Land. Yet, if there is only this single thought and no other thoughts at all—is this not the mind dwelling in meditative concentration?
If one's mindfulness is truly such as this, and one does not see Amitābha, whom else could one see? If one is not born in the Pure Land, where else could one be born?
I fear only that we ourselves lack sufficient self-confidence.
In the *Contemplation Sūtra*, the two phrases "this mind creates the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha" are presented;

once these are raised, it follows that by implication, the mind does not create the Buddha, the mind is not the Buddha, the mind creates the nine realms, the mind is the nine realms, the mind does not create the nine realms, and the mind is not the nine realms—all such meanings are thereby revealed.
Alas! If one clearly understands this principle and yet still does not practice mindfulness of the Buddha, [how can one be said to understand?]
"Then there is nothing I can do for him.

Contemplating these two phrases from the *Contemplation Sutra*—that "this mind creates the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha"—one sees that they are not merely the essential principles and core tenets of the *Contemplation Sutra* alone;
rather, they are truly the great dharma’s fundamental principles throughout the entire lifetime of Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s teaching. Not only [the teachings of] Śākyamuni...

The fundamental principle of the Dharma-treasury of the Buddha Kāśyapa is, in truth, the fundamental principle of the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Once this principle is penetrated, what principle would not be penetrated? Once this Dharma is clarified, what Dharma would not be clarified? As it is said:
"Though one's learning may not be extensive, one may equal the ranks of the superior sages."

The true Dharma has no inherent nature; defilement and purity arise from conditions. Once the single truth is raised, its essence constitutes the ten realms. Thus, the entirety of the ten realms is itself the single truth.
Therefore, those who speak well of the nature of mind and spirit will certainly not abandon cause and effect;
and those who have deep faith in cause and effect will ultimately come to a great illumination of the nature of mind and spirit. This is the inevitable course of principle.
The single thought of the present moment—the mind capable of reciting—is entirely true and yet constitutes delusion; entirely delusive and yet is precisely the truth.

Throughout the day it follows conditions, yet throughout the day it remains unchanging. This single phrase of the Buddha being recited is a name established upon its entirety of virtue; apart from virtue, there is no name.

One invokes virtue by means of names; outside of names, there is no virtue. One is able to contemplate that outside the mind, there is no separate Buddha who is the object of contemplation, and outside the Buddha who is the object of contemplation, there is no separate mind that is the subject of contemplation.
Subject and object are non-dual, yet the birth of the Buddha appears vividly. Fundamentally, they are free from the four extremes.
Fundamentally transcending all negations, fundamentally pervading all things, and fundamentally containing all things, it is absolute, perfectly interfused, and inconceivable.
Practitioners of the Lotus School should enter through faith from this very point.
The act of killing is a transgression of the most profound gravity. All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; how can one kill that which is born?
To commit grave karma, to harbor murderous intent, to bind oneself with deep resentment, and to experience bitter fruits—all these result from this single act of killing.

Consequently, the murderous intent gradually becomes fierce, the karmic retribution of killing gradually deepens, and one proceeds to kill human beings, eventually extending to the slaughter of one's own six kin.
This culminates in the great kalpa of war and weapons; how truly lamentable! This is all brought about by the failure to know the precept against killing.
If one were to know this precept, one would not even bear to kill an animal, let alone a human being, and certainly not one's own kin.
One cannot bear to slaughter sacrificial victims. From where do such great kalpas of weapons and violence originate? He who kills another’s father will have his own father killed by others;
he who kills another’s elder brother will have his own elder brother killed by others. Knowing that one must not kill another’s father or elder brother, [one realizes the same applies to oneself].

This is also a gradual step toward the precept against killing. However, one does not realize that those who kill their fathers and elder brothers do so because they failed to abstain from killing from the outset.
The reason people do not abstain from killing is that they do not comprehend the principle of cause and effect. Cause and effect is the law of resonance:
if I invoke it with an evil mind, others will respond with an evil mind; if I invoke it with a virtuous mind, others will respond with a virtuous mind.
People also respond with a virtuous mind. People know only that cause and response are seen within the present life, yet they do not know that cause and response pervade the three periods of time.
People know only that cause and response are seen within the human realm, yet they do not know that cause and response pervade the six realms of existence.
If one truly knows that cause and response pervade the three periods and the six realms, one will see that throughout the six realms, there have been many lifetimes.
When one kills the father or elder brother, can one not be cautious? Generally, it is known that response and resonance (*ganying*) pervades the six realms of existence;

yet it is also not understood that response and resonance pervades both the mundane and the supramundane. If one responds with a mind free of self, then the fruits of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha will correspond.
If one responds with the Bodhicitta and the myriad practices of the Six Perfections, then the fruit of the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-realm will correspond. By means of...
When moved by impartial great kindness and great compassion of same essence, the fruit of the Buddha-dharma realm responds accordingly. Alas!
How could the way of resonance and response ever be fully described?
One must know that the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha" takes the "mind-only" (cittamātra) as its fundamental principle.

This meaning of mind-only must be established with certainty by means of the three criteria of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). These three criteria are: direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), inference (*anumāna-pramāṇa*), and authoritative testimony (*āptāgama-pramāṇa*). Direct perception refers to the personal realization of the principle.
For example, when the Great Master Kumārajīva was seven years old, he accompanied his mother to a Buddhist temple; upon seeing the Buddha’s alms bowl, he was filled with joy.
He then placed it upon his head. After a short while, he thought to himself, "I am very young, and this Buddha-bowl is extremely heavy.
How can I possibly carry it on my head? As soon as this thought arose, he suddenly let out a cry and set the bowl down. Thereupon, he realized that all phenomena are but the mind alone.
Later, when the Dharma Master Wuiyo of Goryeo came to this land to study, he stayed overnight among the graves. Being very thirsty, he saw a pool of clear water beneath the bright moon.

Wang cupped the water with his hands and drank it; he found it exceptionally fragrant and delicious. When morning came the following day, he saw that the water had emerged from within his tomb, whereupon he felt nauseated and vomited profusely.
He then realized that all phenomena are but the mind (*sarvadharma-mānasamātra*) and returned to his own country to compose his writings.
These were all direct realizations through perception (*pratyakṣa*). As for inference (*anumāna*), one observes the meaning by means of various signs. Inference...
One knows this through analogies. Among all analogies, the analogy of a dream is the most pertinent.
Just as the mountains, rivers, people, and things seen within a dream—however diverse and manifold they may be—do not exist apart from the dreaming mind that perceives them;
outside of that dreaming mind, not a single phenomenon can be found. By this very example, one can understand that all phenomena presently manifest are merely mind alone.

This is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). As for the authority of the sacred word (*āptāgama*), it is said that the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only; thus do thousands of sutras and tens of thousands of treatises declare.

Having already established "mind-only" by means of the three measures—direct perception and so forth—it shall now be further clarified through the two gates of principle (*li*) and phenomenon (*shi*) that [the mind] fully creates [all things].
That is to say, only because there is the fullness of principle can there be the creation of phenomena; if principle were not complete, what would phenomena create? Regarding this...
By means of the principle-endowment (*li-jù*), one merely endows the phenomenal creation (*shi-zào*). Apart from phenomenal creation, there is nothing else that is endowed.

It is because phenomenal creation exists that the principle-endowment is manifested; if phenomena were not created, how could one know of the principle-endowment? Therefore, phenomenal creation is simply the creation of the principle-endowment. Apart from the principle-endowment, there is nothing else created.
Within this single thought-moment, the ten realms and myriad dharmas are inherently endowed. This is...

This single thought-moment, following conditions, is capable of creating the ten realms and myriad phenomena. As for "inherent principle" (*lǐjù*), it is like the inherent principle within gold that it can be fashioned into vessels, basins, hairpins, or bracelets.
As for "actual creation" (*shìzào*), it is like the actual production of vessels, basins, hairpins, or bracelets through the conditions of a craftsman’s furnace and hammer.
Furthermore, as for "inherent principle," it is like the inherent principle within flour that it can be made into various kinds of food.
The production of phenomena is like the conditions of water, fire, human skill, and labor, which result in the creation of various kinds of food.

Having already distinguished between phenomena and principle, we shall further examine and determine the true and the false by means of the identity or difference between names and essence. Within the Buddha-dharma, there are cases where the name is the same but the essence is different.
There are cases where names differ but the substance is the same, and cases where names are the same but the substances differ. For example, regarding the single term "mind" (*citta*):

there is the "fleshly ball of mind," the "mind that cogitates and considers," the "mind that accumulates and arises," and the "solid, essential mind. The fleshly ball of mind is identical to the external four great elements;

it possesses no capacity for cognition or knowledge. The mind that cogitates and considers pervades all eight consciousnesses, because all eight types of consciousness are capable of cogitating and considering their respective objects.

Because it is an object. This refers to the mind that falsely accumulates and arises; this applies exclusively to the eighth [consciousness], because it can accumulate the seeds of all phenomena and can give rise to the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of all phenomena.
This, then, is the union of the true and the false. As for the "firm and real mind," this is the nature of firm and true reality;
it is the numinous awareness free from thought, the essence of the pure true mind. What is now called "mind-only" is...
It is the heart that is firm, solid, and pure. Regarding "different names but the same essence":

the various ultimate designations taught in the various sūtras—such as *tathatā* (Suchness), Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*)—are all this very heart that is firm, solid, and pure.
Having already distinguished the real from the false, we now return to the originally present [nature] to provide a definitive identification. For all the sūtras state:

The true mind has existed from the beginningless beginning. Now, if it is said to have existed from the beginningless beginning, how could it not exist right now? That which exists presently is precisely that which has existed from the beginningless beginning.
If there were no beginningless beginning, there would be no present manifestation; and if one were to depart from the present manifestation, how could there be a beginningless beginning?
Therefore, there is no need to exalt the existence from the beginningless beginning or to trace it back to a remote past; it is simply the self-nature of the single thought-moment of the present.
