This is precisely the originally existent true mind. Because this present single thought-moment is entirely true yet constitutes delusion, and entirely delusive yet is itself true, it follows conditions all day long while remaining unchanging all day long.
Apart from this present single thought-moment, how could there be a separate true mind or self-nature?
As an ancient worthy said: "That which lies beyond the limit of Vipaśyin Buddha is not separate from the gateway of the present world; it is the active functioning of sentient beings."

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is, in fact, the very essence of the immovable wisdom (*akṣobhya-jñāna*) of all Buddhas; one may say they are nearly identical. Through the four preceding meanings, the principle of "Mind-Only" (*cittamātra*) is revealed;
therefore, the first [section] takes Mind-Only as its central tenet. Furthermore, the single phrase "Amitābha" takes the Buddha alone as its central tenet.

Since all phenomena (*dharmas*) are manifested solely by the mind, they are in their entirety nothing but mind. Within the mind, there is no distinction of self and other, nor is there any separation.

Regarding the boundaries: among the myriad phenomena of the ten realms—whether conditioned bases (*āśraya*) or the supported (*āśrita*), whether provisional names or substantial dharmas—whichever single phenomenon one picks up is the entire body of the mind and possesses the great function of the mind.
It is as pervasive horizontally as the mind and as exhaustive vertically as the mind, established by the principle of "mind-only.
Thus, it is only form, only sound, only fragrance, only taste, only touch, and only mental objects, even down to the most minute atom.
Dust is but a mustard seed; when all things are established as being "only meaning," then for the first time the principle of "Mind-Only" is truly realized.
If the principle that "all things are only meaning" were not established, there would be only the empty name of "Mind-Only" without the actual reality of Mind-Only.
Because all things are established as being only meaning, it is said that dharmas have no fixed characteristics and take on their substance according to conditions.

Even a mere mote of dust or a single mustard seed can be taken as the primary tenet; why, then, should Amitābha—the fruition-ground adorned with the eighty thousand marks and signs—not likewise be taken as the primary tenet?
Therefore, we take "only the Buddha" as the primary tenet, and furthermore, we take "absolute, perfect interfusion" as the primary tenet.
Within the myriad dharmas of the ten realms, whichever dharma one may grasp, it is none other than the entire substance of the mind, fully endowed with the greatness of the mind.
It functions horizontally to pervade the ten directions and vertically to exhaust the three periods of time. It is free from the four propositions and transcends the hundred negations.

Its singular essence is entirely true, with nothing existing outside it. Pervasive and pure, there is no room for anything else within it. Since this is so for a single dharma, it is likewise for all dharmas.
Each, when considered in its own essence, is independent and without exterior; this is what is meant by "transcending dependence. Furthermore, regarding the ten realms and the myriad...
Dharmas are each mutually pervasive; each mutually contains the others. They interlace one by one and penetrate one another through and through.

Each and every one is without obstruction or hindrance; each remains unimpaired and unmixed with the others. It is like a single ancient mirror in which images appear in successive layers, or like the thousand jewels of Indra’s net, revolving and mutually encompassing one another.
This, when considering all dharmas in relation to one another, is what constitutes "perfect interfusion" (*yuanrong*). Now...

The synthesis of the absolute (juedai) and the perfect fusion (yuanrong) constitutes a single school. At the very moment of being absolute, it is precisely the perfect fusion; at the very moment of being the perfect fusion, it is precisely the absolute.
It is not that the perfect fusion exists separately apart from the absolute, nor does the absolute exist separately apart from the perfect fusion.
The absolute is its perfect fusion, and the perfect fusion is its absolute. Within this absolute-perfect fusion, each is ultimately ineffable.
It is inconceivable. Now, when these are combined into a single school, it is the "inconceivable within the inconceivable. Furthermore, its tenet is to transcend emotion and leave behind views;
for it concerns the absolute non-relation of all phenomena, which is free from fault and devoid of negation.

Thus, it has already transcended the emotional, deluded attachments of all sentient beings, as well as the various distinctions in the visions of the worthy and sage practitioners of the Three Vehicles. If one considers the perfect interfusion of all phenomena, it is perfectly...
These four statements synthesize and harmonize the "hundred negations" (*śata-apoha*), which is particularly beyond the reach of ordinary sentiments or saintly views.

Therefore, they collectively establish "transcending sentiment and departing from view" as the central tenet. First, "Mind-Only" is established as the tenet; second, "Buddha-Only" is established as the tenet; third, "unconditioned perfect interfusion" is established as the tenet;
and finally, "transcending sentiment and departing from view" is established as the tenet. These four successive layers of fundamental tenets constitute the whole.
This alone constitutes the orthodox lineage of the Single Phrase Amitābha; how could its essential principle be easily explained?

This Dharma-gate of the single thought-moment is like the sky that universally covers all, and like the earth that universally supports all; there is not a single person nor a single dharma that is excluded.

To be able to transcend these and not remain within them—as in the entire *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—although it distinguishes between the five periods and four divisions, the two characters "cause" (*hetu*) and "fruit" (*phala*) encompass everything without exception.
Among the causal minds of the forty-one stages, there is not a single mind that does not incline toward the fruit-consciousness.
Are not the various Dharma-practices cultivated throughout these forty-one stages all nothing but mindfulness?
This is the practice of the Buddha-dharma. Yet, at the very end, Samantabhadra leads [the practitioner] back to Sukhāvatī by means of the ten great kings of vows;
does this not constitute the grand conclusion of the entire scripture? Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* uses the flowers of myriad practices as causes to adorn the fruit of the One Vehicle Buddhahood.
Are these myriad practices not the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha? The *Avataṃsaka* includes the woman Puṣpamitrā; [is she not a manifestation of the Buddha?]...
The King of Disgust (Rājā-nirveda), the Brahmin Jvalanāmukha, and others—through these and countless other gateways—all reveal the realm of Vairocana.

Are these not, in fact, the gateway of Buddha-remembrance? Throughout the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, from beginning to end, there is nothing that does not reveal, awaken, and lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Is this not, from start to finish, the singular gateway of the Buddha-dharma of Buddha-remembrance? The *Laṅkāvatāra*...

The first part, "The Manifestation of the Original Nature," reveals the true cause for attaining Buddhahood. The second part, "The Selection of the Perfect Penetration," demonstrates the wondrous practice for attaining Buddhahood.
The final part, "Traversing the Sixty Holy Stages," shows the fulfillment of Bodhi and the return to non-attainment, which is the realization of the ultimate fruit of the Buddha-ground.
To turn away from this leads to the sinking and wandering within the seven realms of existence; to turn toward this brings clarity.

The five māras cause disturbance. At the end, it says: "If there is a person who has committed the four grave offenses (*catur-guru-dharma*) and the ten *pārājika* transgressions, in a mere instant they will pass through this world and other worlds, even into the Avīci hell, and shall experience all the uninterrupted hells throughout the ten directions until their exhaustion.
Yet, if such a person can, for even a single thought-moment, take up this Dharma-door and reveal it to those who have not yet studied it during the final age, that person’s sins—"
Obstacles should be extinguished through mindfulness; the causes for suffering in the hells are transformed into a land of peace and bliss.
This, then, is the Dharma-door of the Buddha’s Name, which from beginning to end is solely this single practice.

Throughout the entirety of the Buddha’s lifetime teachings—the Three Baskets and Twelve Divisions, the provisional and the real, the partial and the perfect, the sudden and the gradual—all various Dharma-doors are nothing other than the manifestation of the self-nature of the mind alone.
It is simply the nature of perfecting unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment. Is this not, in essence, the single Great Dharma-gate of the Buddha-mindfulness?
As for the arrival of the Great Master Bodhidharma from the West in the Chan school, he merely said: "Directly pointing to the human mind; seeing one's nature is itself liberation."
As for the claim that one "attains Buddhahood," is this not the Zen school as well as the Nianfo (Buddha-recitation) school? Therefore, the two traditions and five houses are unified;
the seventeen hundred public cases (*gong'an*) do nothing more than point directly to the fundamental source-nature of the person and reveal the primordially existing, pure *dharmakāya*.
This *dharmakāya* extends horizontally and penetrates vertically, pervading everywhere without exception. Yet, a practitioner of Chan must at all times...
At that moment, it manifests before one; every single thing is in accord with it. Where, then, is there anything that is not the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance?

As for such expressions as "I do not like hearing the single word 'Buddha'" or "Strike him once with a staff and feed him to the dogs," these all reveal the supreme and wondrous expedient means directed toward the Dharmakāya; this is true Buddha-remembrance. Yet, ignorant people often claim—

It is said that those within the Chan school (Zongmen) should not practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name (*nianfo*). This view not only shows a lack of understanding regarding *nianfo*, but how could it possibly constitute a true knowledge of the Chan school?

Not only is this the case for both the doctrinal and Chan schools, but throughout the world—including the various classes of scholar, farmer, artisan, and merchant, as well as the masters of the hundred schools—whether they wish to recite the Buddha’s name or not, and whether they know of the Buddha or not, none can transcend the Dharma-gate of *nianfo*.
Externally, all coming and going, movement and stillness, follow this Way; the common people use it daily yet remain unaware of it. As the saying goes:
"The single Qi speaks not, yet contains all forms; where could the myriad spirits go to escape its impartiality?
After wind and rain have passed over the peach blossoms by the roadside, there is no place for horse hooves to avoid the remaining petals.
1. To resolve to attain Bodhicitta for the sake of transcending birth and death is the common path for studying the Way. 2.

To uphold the Buddha’s name through deep faith and aspiration constitutes the orthodox tradition of the Pure Land school. 3. To recite with a concentrated and focused mind serves as the expedient means for beginners.
4. To subdue active afflictions (*kleśa*) is the essential task in cultivating the mind. 5. To steadfastly maintain the four grave precepts...
1. The precepts serve as the foundation for entering the Way. 2. Various ascetic practices serve as auxiliary conditions for cultivating the Way. 3.
A single mind without distraction serves as the ultimate destination for purifying one's conduct. 4. Various spiritual omens serve as verification of rebirth in the Pure Land.
These eight matters should each be explained with great care; those who cultivate the karma of purity must not remain ignorant of them.
That sentient beings transmigrate is due to the six realms of existence.

Sentient beings in the other destinies are obstructed by fear, anger, suffering, and pleasure, leaving them no leisure to turn toward the Way and rectify their mental faculties to advance toward Bodhi; only the human realm is capable of this. However—
Those who lose the human body are as numerous as the soil of the great earth; those who obtain the human body are as rare as the soil upon a fingernail.

How difficult it is to obtain a human body! For sentient beings in the human realm, from birth through youth to old age and death, everything seen by the eyes and heard by the ears is nothing other than the worldly dust of toil and the karmic conditions of birth and death. How difficult it is to hear the Buddha-dharma! To obtain—
A human body is already difficult to obtain; how much more so is it to obtain a male body with all six faculties intact. To hear the Buddha-dharma is already difficult;
how much more so is it to hear the name of Amitābha and the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
How fortunate to have obtained this rare human body! How fortunate to have heard this rare Buddha-dharma! Having heard it, if one still refuses to believe, one does not take it deeply to heart.
How lamentable it is! Let us set aside for a moment those who do not believe. Even among those who do believe, to believe without wishing is equivalent to not believing at all.
To wish without acting is equivalent to not wishing at all. To act without vigor is equivalent to not acting at all. The reason one’s action lacks vigor is that one’s wish is not earnest;
the reason one’s wish is not earnest is that one’s belief is not true. In short, [it all depends on] generating true [belief].
Faith is difficult; yet if faith is genuine, it is indeed attained. Vows are difficult; yet if vows are earnest, they are indeed fulfilled.

Practice becomes naturally vigorous when true and earnest faith and vows are augmented by the power of courageous action. One will certainly attain birth in the Pure Land; one will certainly behold Amitābha.
One will certainly realize the three non-regressions; one will certainly attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime.
Once birth in the Pure Land has been secured, the karmic roots of birth and death accumulated over vast kalpas are forever severed from this point on.

Once Buddhahood is attained in a single lifetime, the most supreme and noble, unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment is then fully perfected. How could that which is related to this single thought of true faith be anything other than [this]?

How shallow this is! Were it not for those with thin karmic conditions that obstruct the Way, light karma regarding birth and death, and those who have long planted roots of goodness with profound causes from past lives, how could they be thus?
Yet, throughout immeasurable kalpas, the weight of one's karmic forces and the depth of one's roots of goodness remain entirely unknown.
Nevertheless, karmic forces are transformed by the mind, while roots of goodness depend upon human cultivation. This is so.
Therefore, those who propagate the Dharma must employ skillful means and earnestly provide instruction;

likewise, those who study the Way must exert themselves with diligence and advance resolutely. Yet, even a single word that enters the ear or a single thought that moves the mind can transform karmic forces and cultivate roots of goodness.
Although one may hear various essential instructions, [if they are not applied...]
There is not a single word by which one may enter [the truth]. Even when encountering various conditions of adversity or favor, there has never been so much as a single thought of exertion.
This is because the power of true karma is profound and heavy, while true roots of goodness are slight and sparse; thus, there is simply nothing that can be done about it.
The nature of mind in this very moment is fundamentally of the same substance as that of the Buddhas. The Buddhas have long since awakened to it, yet I remain deluded.
Although the Buddhas have awakened, there is no increase in them; although I remain deluded, there is no decrease in me.

Although the Buddhas have no increase, because they accord with this nature, they experience the great joy of the Dharma; although I have no decrease, because I turn my back on this nature, I undergo the most grievous suffering. The Buddha...

Within the mind-nature of our shared essence, although you experience the bliss of the Dharma, through your great compassion of shared essence and your objectless great kindness, you remember me in every thought-moment and gather and transform me in every thought-moment; I, too, within this mind-nature of our shared essence—
Although you have encountered manifold sufferings, you do not know to look up to the Buddha for refuge, nor do you know to mindfully recollect the Buddha.

You merely pursue sensory objects with your mind and follow your emotions to create karma. Throughout vast eons, what grave karmas—such as the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds—have you not committed?
What great sufferings of the three miserable realms and the eight difficult conditions have you not endured? To speak of this is shameful; reflect upon it!

How terrifying! If you do not now further recollect the Buddha, you will continue as before to bury your head in creating all manner of karma, and you will continue as before to receive all manner of suffering from the very beginning.

Are you not ashamed? Are you not afraid? Now, first recognize that the Buddha, with great kindness and great compassion, remembers and gathers us in for transformation in every thought-moment. Thus, I now feel a profound sense of gratitude for the Buddha’s benevolence.
One should practice mindfulness of the Buddha. Having endured manifold sufferings in vain for long kalpas, one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha because one seeks liberation from suffering.
Since karma already committed cannot be undone, might one not create further karma in the future? One should practice mindfulness of the Buddha by giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse.
If the nature of the mind, which is of the same substance as the Buddha, is said to be inherently present, how could it not exist right now? It is simply that one lacks awakening and realization.
One should practice mindfulness of the Buddha in order to seek awakening to the nature of the mind. Mindfulness of the Buddha must be practiced with earnestness by seeking to awaken the mind.

Mindfulness of the Buddha must be practiced with earnestness by means of a sense of shame and remorse. Mindfulness of the Buddha must be practiced with earnestness by means of a sense of dread and suffering.
Mindfulness of the Buddha must be practiced with earnestness by means of a heart of gratitude. I do not fail to mindfully recollect the Buddha; the Buddha still minds me. Now, I am most earnest.
"Recite the Buddha’s name; the Buddha will surely turn his thought toward you in return. As the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions cherish and remember sentient beings like a mother remembers her child. If the child flees away, what can the mother’s remembrance accomplish?

But if the child remembers the mother as the mother remembers him, then throughout successive lives, mother and child shall not be separated or far apart. If sentient beings with their own minds remember the Buddha and recite his name..."
In the future, you will certainly behold the Buddha; you are not far from him. Without relying on expedient means, you shall spontaneously attain the opening of the mind.
This Great Being has personally realized and reached the ultimate realm; he speaks thus, pouring out his heart and soul to tell you. I now practice the mindfulness of the Buddha.
One will certainly behold the Buddha. Once the Buddha is beheld, one shall be liberated from all sufferings, and the time for awakening will arrive.
If one indeed attains awakening, one may thoroughly cleanse the shame and remorse of the past. How could the Buddha fail to take heed?
All sentient beings are originally Buddhas. The true mind is inherently present; the nature of delusion is fundamentally empty. All wholesome dharmas are by nature spontaneously possessed.

It is only because they have long followed the conditions of delusive defilement that they have not severed the delusion that is fundamentally empty, nor have they realized the truth that is inherently present.
Though the source of goodness is complete, it remains uncultivated; though Buddhahood is original, it remains unaccomplished. Now, wishing to sever this fundamental...
The delusion of emptiness is realized as the truth of original existence; the goodness inherent in nature is cultivated to become the Buddha that has always been.

For those who follow the conditions for awakening to purity, there is no single practice more direct, more exhilarating, more sudden, and more perfect than the single act of reciting the Name while mindful of the Buddha.
For the mind that is capable of mindfulness is originally entirely true yet becomes deluded; entirely deluded, it is... [the entirety of the true].
Truly, the Buddha who is the object of contemplation is also named based on the perfection of his fundamental virtues; the name itself is the virtue.

Apart from the mind that contemplates, there is no separate Buddha who is contemplated; apart from the Buddha who is contemplated, there is no separate mind that contemplates. When both subject and object are forgotten, the mind and the Buddha are as one.
Within every thought-moment, one perfectly subdues and perfectly severs the afflictions of the five abodes, and perfectly transforms and perfectly extinguishes the three [poisons].
It thoroughly destroys the obstacles of affliction; it thoroughly transcends the five turbidities; it thoroughly purifies the four lands; it thoroughly contemplates the three bodies;

it thoroughly cultivates the myriad practices; and it thoroughly realizes the original truth, thereby perfectly accomplishing unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment. If one is thus in a single thought-moment, so it is in every thought-moment.
Provided one can maintain this continuity from thought to thought, the subduing, severing, cultivation, and realization thereof are such that they cannot be grasped by the conceptual mind.

This is what the deliberators have said. To preserve the Buddha’s mind and to contemplate the Buddha who is the complete mind, one truly possesses the full portion of the majestic virtue and spiritual power of the fruition-Buddha within one's own mind, which provides secret, transformative influence and protection.
If one recites a single phrase of the Buddha’s name without admixture of other conditions, and the merit of ten recitations is perfected, one suddenly transcends many kalpas.
To lack faith in this is truly to be like wood or stone; to abandon this and practice otherwise is not [the way].
"Madness is indeed delusion. What more can be said? What more can be said? Question: "All directions possess pure lands.
Why do you exclusively praise the Western Land and urge us to seek rebirth there? Answer: "This is not merely the opinion of a human teacher;
it is the sincere word from the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha], clearly pointing the way. Thus, it is stated in various Mahāyāna sūtras of both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings."
Because they share the same ultimate goal, it causes those of initial resolve to focus single-mindedly on a single object, whereby samādhi is easily accomplished.

Because the Forty-Eight Vows serve as the condition (*pratyaya*), the condition is powerful; because the ten recitations serve as the cause (*hetu*), the cause is supreme; and because there is a particular affinity between the Buddha and sentient beings.
For the sentient beings of this land—regardless of whether they are monastics or laypeople, male or female, old or young, virtuous or evil—when they are in that state...
At times when one encounters conditions of extreme favor or adversity, suffering or joy, these feelings will most often arise from within and burst forth from the mouth.
One might utter a single invocation of the Buddha's name; yet, if one does not invoke the Buddha, that is that. Whenever one invokes the Buddha, it must be Amitābha Buddha whom one invokes.
Who causes this to be so? It is because sentient beings have long been transformed by the Buddha’s influence, have long received the Buddha’s grace, and share a deep affinity with the Buddha.

Furthermore, this *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* was first translated by Kumārajīva. The patriarch Huiyuan of Donglin immediately formed a religious society (*śamatha-saṃgha*) with one hundred and twenty-three people to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
These one hundred and twenty-three people were gradually transformed over time;

at the end of their lives, they all left behind auspicious signs. Even when the parrot, the eight-eight children, and others recited the Buddha’s name, they each manifested auspicious omens at the time of their passing. This is...
It is not that sentient beings have a particularly deep affinity with the Buddha; what, then, is the reason? Furthermore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:

"When the future teachings of the scriptures are extinguished, I shall, by the power of my vows, specifically preserve this sūtra so that it remains for another hundred years to extensively deliver all conscious beings.
Now, as for why other sūtras are not preserved while only this one is retained—could it not be because this Dharma-gate is easy to take up and practice?

It encompasses all capacities; entry into the Way is stable and the attainment of benefit is swift. By this one may know that the later the time, the more this Dharma accords with the needs of those capable of receiving it.
When sentient beings of the world encounter times of urgent distress and suffering, they wail for their parents and cry out to Heaven and Earth;

yet they do not realize that their parents, humans, kings, or gods cannot save them from birth and death or bring an end to their saṃsāra, because they themselves remain within the cycle of birth and death.
Although the noble ones of the Three Vehicles have transcended birth and death, they lack the heart of great compassion.

It is of no benefit to me. Although the various Bodhisattvas possess great compassion, because their respective realizations have limitations, they are unable to universally benefit all sentient beings or fulfill all their aspirations.
Although the Buddhas of the ten directions have all realized the ultimate extent of the Dharma-realm, it is not easy for me to evoke their response;
even if I were to evoke it to the utmost and behold them, I would merely experience a temporary relief from suffering, and in the end—
This is not the ultimate. Only with Amitābha Buddha—if one but obtains a single vision—is there immediate liberation from birth and death, and the eternal severing of the root of suffering.
This single phrase, "Amitābha Buddha," is that which one must devote one's whole heart and all one's strength to.
As I have previously said in verse: "Having thoroughly contemplated the mundane and the supramundane, if one does not call upon Amitābha, whom else would one call upon? Yet, one must call upon him...
It is not difficult for the Buddha; the difficulty lies in persistence.

If one can truly maintain a single thought with such firmness that it is as if cast from raw iron or forged from solid steel—if one is like a single person facing ten thousand enemies, whom a thousand sages cannot obstruct and ten thousand oxen cannot turn back—then after a long time, one will surely achieve resonance and correspondence.
If one is unable to apply the mind in this manner, then...
To say that the Buddha’s words lack efficacy, or that the Buddha’s mind is difficult to move, is surely impossible.

Yet, by attaining a single moment of resonance and penetration, one may suddenly transcend birth and death, ascend directly to the stage of non-retrogression, and securely realize the fruit of Buddhahood—is this not a most extraordinary thing?
To know the small while not knowing the great, and to see the near while not seeing the far—this is the common lot of sentient beings.
For example, Amitābha Buddha possesses great benevolence and virtue toward all sentient beings, yet sentient beings do not recognize it.
Countless eons ago, before the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, Amitābha made four vows for the sake of suffering sentient beings in the evil world.
Regarding the eighteen kinds of great vows: relying upon these vows, he practiced the bodhisattva path for many long kalpas.
He gave up the position of a golden-wheel-turning monarch, his kingdom, cities, wives, and children, as well as his head, eyes, brain, and marrow—countless hundreds of thousands of millions of times.

This is but a single instance of the giving of internal and external wealth among the ten thousand practices. Likewise, there were acts of forbearance that others cannot endure, and deeds performed that others cannot...

They are able to practice. They cultivate the myriad practices to perfection; their power reaches its limit and their merit becomes pure. They adorn and complete a Pure Land and personally attain Buddhahood.

They manifest infinite emanations to welcome and guide sentient beings, employing skillful means to gather and transform them, causing them to be born in that land. Thus, it is as if they were acting for the sake of a single person.
It is the same for the multitude. As it is for the multitude, so it is for a single person. If one views it from the perspective of the multitude, the Buddha acts universally for all sentient beings;
if one views it from the perspective of a single person, the Buddha acts specifically for me alone.
His great vows, which accord with the nature of reality, were made for my sake. His great practices throughout long kalpas were cultivated for my sake. The four lands...
I am the one who purifies and adorns. The three bodies are my fulfillment.
Thus, he manifests his form in every instance to guide and receive beings, and displays auspicious responses everywhere; all of this is for my sake. When I create karma, the Buddha awakens me.
When I undergo suffering, the Buddha rescues me. When I take refuge, the Buddha accepts me. When I practice the path...
At that time, the Buddha bestowed his grace upon me.

All the various ways in which the Buddha has acted for my sake have been nothing other than his desire for me to mindfully recollect the Buddha, his desire for me to attain rebirth in the Pure Land, his desire for me to be forever liberated from all suffering and extensively receive the joy of the Dharma, and his desire for me to successively transform and deliver all sentient beings until I finally reach the stage of being one life away from Buddhahood. Alas! The Buddha...
This profound kindness and weighty virtue cannot be compared to that of one's parents; even heaven and earth are insufficient to illustrate its height and depth.
Had I not heard this instruction, how could I have known this meaning? Had I not read the Buddhist scriptures, how could I have understood this principle?

From this day forward, I already know it. I shall only exert all my strength in diligent cultivation, repaying this grace with total sincerity, and risk my very life in the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
That being so, what more need be said?

All sentient beings are driven by the ten afflictions (daśa-āsrava), both sharp and dull; for long kalpas they have wandered through birth and death, undergoing great suffering and distress, unable to escape.

How lamentable this is! What are these ten afflictions? They are: the view of a self (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), extreme views (antagrāha-dṛṣṭi), false views (mithyā-dṛṣṭi), attachment to views (dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa), attachment to precepts and vows (śīla-vrata-parāmarśa),... [and so forth].

These five are the sharp fetters (*tīkṣṇa-anuśaya*), because they are active and agile. Greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt—these five are the dull fetters (*mṛdu-anuśaya*), as they are produced by the sharp fetters;
thus, the dull are spoken of in contrast to the sharp. Among sentient beings, these ten fetters are present in varying degrees, each having its own particular predominance.
If one practices the path while carrying these along, it will only cause the increase of false views and afflictions; there is absolutely no [possibility of liberation].
The Section on Correspondence (*saṃprayukta-bhāga*). It is truly difficult to sever [the afflictions] as they correspond [to their objects].

By means of these ten proclivities (*anuśaya*), throughout the four truths across the nine stages of the three realms, there are eighty-eight proclivities of the delusions of view (*darśana-heya*) and eighty-one grades of the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

To sever merely the delusions of view is like cutting off a current forty *li* long; how much more so for the delusions of cultivation? If even a hair’s breadth of either the two delusions—view or cultivation—remains unexhausted, one remains subject to the cycle of birth and death (*bhavacakra*).
One cannot escape from birth and death; this is what is called "ascending out of the three realms. It is extremely difficult, indeed most difficult.

Now, these ten afflictions (*daśa-āsrava*) are collectively termed the "cognitive vision of sentient beings" (*sattva-jñāna-dṛṣṭi*). The ancient masters taught that the cognitive vision of sentient beings must be remedied by the "cognitive vision of the Buddha" (*buddha-jñāna-dṛṣṭi*).
This cognitive vision of the Buddha is precisely the numinous awareness (*ling-zhi*) present before one, free from discursive thought. However, this numinous awareness [cannot...]

To stand alone and independent, one must necessarily arise in accordance with conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*). If one does not follow the conditions of the Buddha-realm, one will instead follow the conditions of the nine realms.

Outside of these ten realms, there is no separate arising of conditions. If one wishes to follow the conditions of the Buddha-realm, there is nothing like upholding the Buddha’s name with a mind of faith and aspiration.
However, faith values depth, aspiration values urgency, and the upholding of the name values single-minded diligence. The fruit [is attained] through this depth.
With a mind of total dedication and diligence, one holds the name with faith and aspiration; this is precisely to take the Buddha’s knowledge and vision as one’s own knowledge and vision.
It is also, in every moment of thought, to use the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to treat the knowledge and vision of sentient beings.

Within the burning heart of the ten afflictions (*kleśa*), simply place the single-minded resolve of holding the name with faith and aspiration; thus, the dependent origination of the realm of birth-and-death is transformed into the dependent origination of the Buddha-realm.
Arise! Within this gateway of the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), this is the most wondrous method for transforming iron into gold.

It requires only that you shoulder the burden with naked integrity, persevering without ceasing for a long time. You may be certain that you can sit in wait for the Golden Terrace, and before long, the precious lotus will come to welcome you.
This is to depart from this cohabitation and be born into that cohabitation, emerging horizontally from the triple world.
Compared to those who emerge vertically, is this not indeed a saving of effort?
A single utterance of "Amitābha Buddha" is the *agada* medicine that cures every ailment; it is the king of wish-fulfilling jewels that fulfills every aspiration;
it is the compassionate vessel that ferries one across the bitter sea of birth and death, delivering all who suffer;
it is the lamp of wisdom in the long night of ignorance, dispelling every darkness. To have this name once pass through the faculty of hearing is to possess a karmic affinity; if one can merely...
A single thought of faith is sufficient for attunement with the Way. If this faith is genuine, vows will arise spontaneously without being sought.

One should simply maintain these two dharmas—faith and vow—constantly within the mind, like a loyal minister receiving the secret edicts of a sagacious sovereign, or a filial son receiving the solemn command of a compassionate father.
Remembering them without forgetfulness, one should treat them as the foremost essential matter, regardless of other circumstances.

Whether one’s circumstances are in a quiet or bustling place, whether one is at leisure or in haste, and whether one has many thoughts or few—these are all, in their entirety, the primary causes for rebirth in the Pure Land.
One need only fear that they depend upon the interval between diligence and indolence.

Since we have been in saṃsāra for vast eons, how could we never have given rise to the mind seeking liberation and cultivated the practices directed toward the Way? It is simply that we have all neglected them through complacency and failed because of...
Laziness is why one constantly remains within birth and death, undergoing great suffering and affliction.

Now that you have heard this concise Dharma-door of holding the Name, if you still follow your old ways and remain complacent in your ruin, you may be called the foremost of those lacking any spirit of manhood.
What is called "upholding the name" refers to that which is described as "reverently wearing it upon one's breast. It means to hold it firmly in the mind without momentarily forgetting it.
If there is even a single thought of interruption, it is not upholding; if there is even a single thought of admixture, it is not upholding.
For thoughts to continue in succession, without admixture and without interval—this is true diligence; this is diligence.
If one does not cease, one will gradually enter the state of single-mindedness without distraction and fully accomplish pure karma.

If one reaches this state of single-mindedness without distraction and continues to practice with diligence without interruption, one will soon see wisdom opened, eloquence inspired, and supernormal powers attained.
One will achieve the Buddha-remembrance samādhi, and various miraculous and auspicious signs will all manifest before one. It is like a wax figure being held toward a fire; where it is thin...
Practice first; however, one must not harbor a mind that anticipates immediate results. One should simply apply oneself to the state of "single-mindedness without distraction.
Single-mindedness without distraction is the ultimate destination of pure practice and the great gateway to the Pure Land.
If one does not enter this gate, one will ultimately find no stability. May students not fail to exert themselves!
In the cultivation of all dharma-gates, what is valued is clarifying the fundamental principle and attaining the ultimate meaning. People today know only that the myriad dharmas are but mind;
they do not know that the mind is but the myriad dharmas. They know only that there is no Buddha outside the mind; they do not know that there is no mind outside the Buddha.
They know only that the infinite is one; they do not know that the one is the infinite. They know only how to transform mountains, rivers, and the great earth back into themselves.
One does not realize that it is one's own self that transforms into the mountains, rivers, and the great earth.

Since one does not know that the mind is nothing other than the myriad dharmas, how can one truly know that the myriad dharmas are nothing other than the mind? Since one does not know that there is no mind outside the Buddha, how can one truly know that there is no Buddha outside the mind?
This is what is meant by a single perfect sphere split into two halves: if separated, both are damaged; if joined, both are beautiful.
Therefore, those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha must take "only the Buddha and only the land" as their fundamental principle.

If this principle of "only the Buddha and only the land" is not clarified, then the meaning of True Mind-Only will not be established. Once the meaning of True Mind-Only is thoroughly penetrated, the principle of "only the Buddha and only the land" is naturally realized.
Having established this principle, then the single phrase of the Buddha being mindful of and the land being born from are entirely—

The essence is vast in its function; it extends horizontally and exhausts the vertical [axis]. Its singular substance is entirely true, encompassing all without exterior. Since that which is contemplated is thus, so too is the contemplating subject.
This is called contemplating the Buddha of Real-Phase (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) with the mind of Real-Phase; contemplating the Buddha of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) with the mind of the Dharma-realm.
Each thought-moment is free from dependence; each thought-moment is perfectly interfused. Because they are free from dependence, they completely transcend all dharma-gates. There is none...

Regarding "being equal": because of its perfect interfusion, it fully encompasses all dharma-gates, with nothing existing outside of it. This is what is meant by "dharmas having no fixed characteristics.
When meeting conditions, they immediately become the central principle; their vast functions flourish profusely, and every action necessarily manifests the absolute truth.
A single phrase, "Amitābha Buddha," must be believed and recited in this manner; only then is it the inconceivable within the inconceivable.
The Buddha and sentient beings are non-dual; that which they equally and universally possess is nothing other than this present, thought-free, numinous awareness.
Buddhas, by virtue of the causes and conditions of awakening, awaken again and again, purify again and again, until the ultimate limit of awakening and purification is reached;

thus their numinous awareness extends horizontally and exhausts the vertically, vast and without exterior. Sentient beings, by virtue of the causes and conditions of delusion and defilement, become deluded...
Furthermore, it is deluded again and again, and defiled again and again; thus its numinous awareness is constricted and hurried, becoming merely a faint and inferior state.
Nevertheless, this very faint and inferior numinous awareness is, in its essential substance, non-dual with the vast numinous awareness of all Buddhas, without the slightest difference.
If one encounters conditions for awakening to purity, such that karma is exhausted and afflictions are emptied, then this faint and inferior awareness—
At that moment, it transforms into a vast, all-encompassing spiritual awareness. It is like a single spark of fire that can burn ten thousand acres of wasteland.
Yet, regarding this present moment of spiritual awareness, if one considers the objects known, there are indeed differences in breadth, narrowness, excellence, and inferiority;
however, if one considers the knowing itself, it is in its entirety without distinction—just as a single [spark is no different from the fire it produces].
It is fire. When sandalwood is burned, it is fragrant; when excrement is burned, it is foul-smelling. Although that which is burned differs, the fire that burns it is not two.
Furthermore, it is like water: though clear and turbid differ, they are the same water. It is like a mirror: though dim and bright vary, they are the same mirror.
Although clear and turbid are distinct, the nature of moisture is non-dual. Although dim and bright differ, the essence of light is the same. Water is uniformly moist; [the turbid...]
That which is turbid can be made clear by purifying it; the mirror and its light are one and the same. That which is obscured can be made bright by polishing it.
When the light is obscured, it is merely because of the presence of grime; the grime is not the light, for the light is the very essence of the mirror. As for turbid water...
It is merely defiled by dust; yet dust is not moisture. Moisture is the fundamental nature of water.
This single thought of numinous awareness is like the moisture of water, the radiance of a mirror, or the burning of fire—it is uniform throughout its entire being without distinction.

Precisely because it is uniform throughout its entire being without distinction, there are many gates within the skillful means of the path of cultivation. There are those who merely look up with admiration toward all...
O Holy One, there are those who honor only their own spiritual essence; there are those who outwardly admire the various sages while inwardly valuing their own spiritual essence;

and there are those who neither admire the various sages nor value their own spiritual essence. If one merely looks up to and admires the various sages—such as a person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha according to their original lot—they do so because they know that all sages have already previously realized their own spiritual essence, and that in every word, silence, movement, or stillness, [it is this very essence].
This serves as a worthy model for emulation. If we do not look up to and admire the various sages, there will be no path for our progress and cultivation.

Therefore, some exclusively uphold the Name, while others visualize their voices and countenances; with the three karmas in sincere devotion, they pay reverent homage throughout the six periods of the day, surrendering their hearts and taking refuge.
One fulfills one's debt of gratitude by following and upholding [the teachings]. When the time arrives and conditions ripen, the resonance between the Way and the individual intermingles;

the ground of the mind opens wide, and the numinous light shines forth alone. One then realizes that one’s own spiritual essence is fundamentally equal to that of all the sages, without distinction, and thus one must not fail to respect it.
Furthermore, as for merely respecting one’s own spiritual essence, consider those who practice Chan in the Zen school: they take direct pointing as their method.

The human mind sees its nature and attains Buddhahood. Therefore, one simply desires that throughout the twelve hours of the day and within the four modes of deportment, the face of the person itself be revealed alone, experiencing the natural splendor of the original ground.
Apart from this mind-nature, there is nothing at all to grasp or cling to. As it is said: "Let a thousand sages appear as they may;
I possess the Buddha of True Birth. When one's practice has reached profound depth and realization is perfected, [the truth is fully manifest].
One thus realizes that all the sages have long since already realized one’s own numinous spirit; this is something one must especially admire.
Furthermore, regarding those who look outwardly to the sages while inwardly valuing their own numinous spirit: to truly honor one's own numinous spirit, one must necessarily admire the sages;
yet, it is precisely through this admiration of the sages that one honors one's own numinous spirit. Moreover, as for this admiration...
All sages must necessarily respect their own spirits. If one does not respect one's own spirit, how can one admire the sages?

This is the simultaneous cultivation of the internal and external; when the mind and the Buddha are equally valued, there is no partiality or attachment, and progress on the Path becomes ever more rapid.

When one reaches the ultimate limit of power and the purity of achievement, such that the whole body is in resonance, one then realizes that all sages are nothing other than those who have first realized my own self.
It is spirit alone. There is no need for admiration. As for my own spirit, it is merely equal and identical to that of all the sages;

why labor to revere it? Furthermore, one who does not admire the sages and does not revere their own spirit is said to be "unclad by even a single thread," where mind and Buddha are both forgotten, completely cast off, and utterly without dependence. Externally, the world is abandoned; internally...

Liberating body and mind, not a single thought arises; ten thousand conditions are severed at once. When, after a long time, one’s practice has matured and one enters into perfect realization, the original spirit is revealed alone, and all sages are suddenly equalized.
Although one does not look up with admiration for the sages, this is the true way of admiring them;

although one does not hold one’s own spirit in high esteem, this is the true way of honoring it. Regarding these four paths, let the student personally examine their own capacity and disposition. Each...
Follow whatever you prefer; simply enter deeply through a single gate. After a long time, you will surely find resonance with all of them.
You must by no means give rise to arbitrary attachments or rashly engage in debate, shifting from one position to another, asserting that this is right while rejecting the rest.
Not only will this turn your back on the wondrous Way and create obstacles, but it may even lead to slandering the Great Dharma and incurring grave transgressions.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "That which is known by all the sages is transmitted from one to another: that false discrimination has no intrinsic nature. The Second Patriarch said:
"When seeking the mind, it is utterly unattainable. The *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states: "If there is one who can contemplate non-thought, they are thereby heading toward Buddha-wisdom.
The *Huayan He Lun* states: "To suddenly awaken to the fact that a single thought-moment is a conditionally arisen non-arising is to transcend the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles."

The study of Right View—whether in the Buddha’s sutras, the patriarchs’ words, the bodhisattvas, or the treatises composed by spiritual friends—all point directly to the single thought-moment of the present, revealing that the nature of delusion is fundamentally empty.
Now, if delusion is fundamentally empty while the True is fundamentally existent, who else could this be but the Buddha?
It is only that sentient beings have long followed defiled conditions and have thus been unable to suddenly restore their original emptiness.

One must gradually transform them by means of pure dependent origination. By taking my own mind as the causal Buddha and contemplating the resultant Buddha within my own mind, cause and effect have always been mutually penetrating;
the mind and the Buddha are naturally and inherently one and the same. And so, the resultant Buddha within my own mind—
The unconditional great kindness and the great compassion of shared essence are inherently inconceivable.

Furthermore, my very mind as a cause for Buddhahood—my profound faith, earnest aspiration, and single-minded, sincere recitation of the Name—is likewise inconceivable; for within every thought-moment, it is able to...
It purifies all defilements and perfectly reveals original emptiness; it suddenly accords with the numinous source and proceeds directly toward the ocean of fruition.

Thus, there is no condition for purity that surpasses this. However, at the moment of mindfulness, one must let go of the myriad conditions, holding fast to a single thought-moment as if putting out a fire on one’s head, as if mourning the death of one’s parents, as a hen brooding her eggs, or as a dragon nurturing its pearl. One should not expect minor results, nor...
Seek swift accomplishment. Simply maintain this single-minded recitation at all times; this is called the unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous gate of Chan.
Herein, the physical body and the world subtly follow the mind, transforming with every thought-moment, such that it is almost beyond the perception of ordinary minds or the physical eye.
When one's retribution ends and life is exhausted, the holy assembly of Amitābha will suddenly appear before them, or...
Only when various extraordinary fragrances, celestial music, and all manner of auspicious omens appear do worldly people finally claim that their pure karma has been accomplished.
Yet, how could the accomplishment of pure karma truly occur at such a time?

When recollecting the Buddha, one should give rise to four kinds of mind. What are these four? First, realizing that since beginningless time one has created karma leading to this present state, one should give rise to a mind of shame and remorse.
Second, having heard this Dharma-gate, one should give rise to a mind of joy and celebration.

Third, regarding the karmic obstructions from beginningless time and the fact that this Dharma is difficult to encounter and difficult to meet, one should give rise to a mind of sorrow and lamentation. Fourth, [realizing] that the Buddha is thus compassionate, one should give rise to...
A heart of gratitude. Among these four kinds of mind, if even one is present, pure practice can be accomplished. One should practice mindfulness of the Buddha for a long duration;
it must not be interrupted. If interrupted, pure practice cannot be accomplished. One should be persistent for a long duration; one must not be weary or indolent.
If weary or indolent, pure practice cannot be accomplished. If one is persistent but lacks vigor, there will be regression. [Vigor...]
If it is fierce but not enduring, there is no progress.
When recollecting the Buddha, one must not harbor other thoughts. To have no other thoughts is itself *śamatha*. When recollecting the Buddha...

It must be clearly and distinctly understood. To be able to understand clearly and distinctly is itself contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), both tranquility (*śamatha*) and contemplation are fully present;

it is not that tranquility and contemplation exist separately. Tranquility is the cause of concentration (*samādhi*); concentration is the fruit of tranquility. Contemplation is the cause of wisdom (*prajñā*); wisdom is the fruit of contemplation.

When not a single thought arises and one understands clearly and distinctly, this is stillness-with-illumination. Understanding clearly and distinctly within a single thought-moment—[is stillness-with-illumination].
Birth is itself illumination and stillness. One who can act in this way will certainly achieve pure karma without fail. Those who achieve it in this manner are all of the highest grade.
Whether it be one person or even hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, or billions of people, if they practice in this way, they will all achieve such accomplishment.
Those who practice the recitation of the Buddha's name—should they not be cautious?

Compiled by the dharma heirs, Liaomei and others,
from miscellaneous writings on the two great principles of Prajñā and Pure Land.
Prajñā clarifies the emptiness of nature through dependent origination; though it is the emptiness of nature, it does not destroy dependent origination.
Pure Land clarifies dependent origination through the emptiness of nature; though it is dependent origination, it does not obstruct the emptiness of nature.

Thus, these two gates of emptiness and existence do not hinder one another. This is not limited to this alone; it is precisely because of dependent origination that there is the emptiness of nature. If it were not...

Regarding dependent origination: it explains that whatever has the nature of emptiness is precisely why dependent origination is the nature of emptiness. Furthermore, because it is empty by nature, there is dependent origination;
if it were not empty by nature, from what could dependent origination arise? This is precisely why the nature of emptiness is dependent origination.
If this is so, then emptiness and existence constitute two gates that do not merely fail to obstruct one another, but rather mutually establish each other.
As it has been said of old: "The myriad phenomena reach toward heaven; one observes them, yet they have no color. The multitude of sounds resounds across the earth;
one listens to them, yet they have no sound. The more there is, the more empty it becomes; the more empty it becomes, the more there is.

Now, since dependent origination and the emptiness of intrinsic nature function simultaneously and spontaneously, there is the manifestation of both simultaneous cessation and simultaneous preservation. This simultaneous cessation and simultaneous preservation are unimpeded at once.

That the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was written in blood by Zen practitioner Badequan and yet remained efficacious is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
That it was written with a sense of self and yet remained obscure is the knowledge and vision of sentient beings (*sattvajñānadarśana*). Sentient beings...
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision are no different [from those of others]; it is merely the single deluded self that stands between them.

Now, the root of great delusion resides in the self, and among all things most cherished by the self, none surpasses the body. If sentient beings do not eliminate the view of a body and break through the grasping at a self, how can the cycle of birth and death ever cease?
The Chan practitioner De has secretly made nine grades of pure vows; he has recorded this.
He completed the seven-fascicle Lotus Sutra by using the frost-knife of his insentient body to pierce his own blood, which was difficult to draw forth;

his ten fingers were drained dry, yet his mind remained unmoving. How magnificent! Truly, amidst the boundless sea of suffering, he suddenly emptied his self-view and was a heroic man who directly transcended birth and death.
Alas! When a Zen practitioner first conceives this thought, it is like the time when the lotus seeds are being planted.

As the days pass, one gradually transcribes the text; this is the time when the lotus flower grows. When the work of the seven fascicles is perfected, it is the time when the lotus flower is fully endowed with light and fragrance.
Thus, the pure cause of the practitioner of Zen is already established. One need only ensure that the original vow is not forgotten.
Fix your mind on the Buddha and wait until this life’s retribution has ended and the flowers of that land have blossomed;
that will be the time when you see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and the causes and fruits are perfected. Nevertheless, let us now ask the practitioner:

at the very moment the golden knife slices through the flesh and the blood-pen traces its strokes, is it the spirit that knows the pain and forms the characters? Is it ignorance? Is it the self? Or is it not the self?
Is it the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? Or is it the sentient beings’ knowledge and vision? If one understands this clearly, then the Buddha-land is not remote;
the precious lotus will surely blossom. Yet perhaps it has not yet done so. Please take this to heart with clarity, so that you may verify it with the Venerable Amitābha.

At the beginning of the transcription of the Lotus Sūtra in blood by the Chan practitioner Baming, before the golden knife had even been raised and the bamboo pen had been grasped, the entire ten directions were this blood-dripping, wondrous *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
To see through to this point is to say that the assembly on Vulture Peak has never dispersed; it is to say that the assembly on Vulture Peak is fundamentally [present].
It was acceptable that they had never met before; it would have been acceptable to disperse with a shout at that time;

it is also acceptable for them to meet again today. When the Great Function manifests, no fixed rules are maintained. Like a king’s precious sword, killing or giving life is decided according to the occasion.
Thus piercing the blood and thus copying the sutras—this is true diligence; this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata, by which one may give full expression.

The intention of our Original Teacher in appearing in the world was such that he caused the stupas of the Buddhas of antiquity who had entered *nirvāṇa* to directly cause the life-roots of the twelve classes of sentient beings to be severed at a stroke, while making the boundless treasury of Dharma manifest its full literary brilliance with a single stroke of the brush.
Therein, every drop returns to the source and every word captures the marrow; it is not merely that the un-piercable is pierced and the unwritable is written. It unfolds—
It is like adorning fine flowers upon brocade, or pointing out the bright moon at the edge of the sky. Although this monk Mingchan is still young in years, he is sincere in his pursuit of the Way;
he has pricked his own blood to transcribe the sutras and turned his heart toward the Land of Bliss.

That he was able to hear this teaching without giving rise to alarm or fear is proof that he has understood the primary meaning and possesses the causes for rebirth in the superior grade. If this were not the case, one must simply [practice] for twelve [years].
During these times and within the four modes of deportment, by means of the mindfulness of copying the sutras, may you forget all external conditions moment by moment;
with a heart that pierces its own blood, may you remember the Buddha thought after thought. You can certainly expect to sit in wait for the Golden Terrace and hear the wondrous Truth before long.

Otherwise, you will surely see me as the one who copies, and the sutra as the object copied; you will see him as the time of piercing the blood, and him as the place where the sutra is written. By means of this...

To take up the dharma of the true mark with a mind of arising and ceasing, and to transform the practice of non-contempt into a banner of self-conceit (*māna*), is not only a total delusion regarding the wondrous Dharma and a distant背离 (reversal) from the Buddha’s heart;
it is also a profound betrayal of this single point of courageous pure faith, difficult to arouse even over hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes.
How lamentable! May you, O practitioner of Chan, exert yourselves.

"A single ray of light shines eastward, and the ten realms are fully manifested; he manifests bodies according to the species [of beings], and delivers them from suffering in accordance with their thoughts. This is not incorrect, yet it is merely its secondary aspect.

Listen! You must, before the thought has even been raised, directly encounter this Dharma within the state where the World-Honored One could not open his mouth, and at the moment when the Great Being could not avoid it.
At that very instant, you must personally see this Dharma in every phenomenon and this gate in every door; yet, at such a time, do not understand it in such a way.

Only now have I first acquired the eye to behold the scriptures; otherwise, it would be like counting the sands of the ocean or mistaking the finger for the moon—not only would one’s own spirit be buried, but one would also fail to appreciate those with clear vision.
I fear that the Universal Gate will gradually close and the Sublime Dharma will ultimately vanish.
Having perceived this, I, Mo Chao, obtained this sutra and bound it in volumes, appending these few words for the benefit of all who see or hear it.

How could this be the "existence" of the Existence Gate (you-men) of the Perfect Teaching, or the "existence" of the original presence of inherent nature? It is only fitting that they should call it shallow; there is no need for further debate.

"Śūraṅgama" (First Samādhi) is the name of the great samādhi that accords with the nature of reality; it takes the Tathāgatagarbha mind as its essential substance.

Taking the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing as the entryway, and taking the ultimate realization of the stages of sainthood as the final goal—this is based on the principle of the *tathāgatagarbha* nature.
From this, one gives rise to practice that accords with that nature, thereby returning to and realizing the entire substance of the *garbha* nature.

The essential meaning of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is fully exhausted herein; thus, Mañjuśrī requested that the title of the sutra be finalized. Following this, the text further clarifies those who obscure or misunderstand this.

It is inevitable that one will sink into the cycles of the seven realms of existence. Regarding the instruction that those who practice this must guard against the disturbances of the five maras, this merely serves as a foil to highlight the primary teaching, thereby supplementing the essential matters therein.
Within the sutra, the Pure Land is also elucidated; there are four points concerning it.

Reflecting on the Dharma is of the utmost importance. Yet, for a Bodhisattva to cultivate the causes and realize the fruit, benefiting both self and others, all is fully accomplished through *nianfo* (Buddha-recollection) alone.

Now, although at the Stage of Dry Wisdom the five abodes of ignorance are completely suppressed, the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*) have not yet been severed; how then can it be said that [rebirth] does not occur?

This refers to "successive rebirth. It means that one transcends the defiled land of common residence (*sahā-loka*) and is born into the pure land of common residence. Master Zhiyi provides clear evidence for this.

In the third section on the "Rising and Sinking of Sentimental Conceptions," it says: "If one consists purely of conceptions, one will immediately fly upward and will certainly be born in the heavens.
If within the mind of flight there is both merit and wisdom, as well as pure vows, the mind will naturally open and one will see the Buddhas of the ten directions in their purity."

As for the buddha-lands, one will be reborn therein according to one’s vows. While the preceding Stage of Dry Wisdom still belongs to the ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*), this [stage] concerns ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) on the broad ground;
if their minds consist purely of thought, they possess the lot to be reborn there. This is surely due to the great compassionate heart of our Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Within this fiercely burning cycle of saṃsāra, I have specifically extracted and set forth this essential path for transcending the triple world.

Those throughout past and present who, though not yet having entered the stage of sainthood, attained rebirth in the Pure Land at the moment of death—these are its witnesses. Within the fourth section, the *Parīndanā* (Distribution), it is said:
"If there is a person who possesses grave offenses and is about to encounter extreme evil, yet in a single thought-moment promotes the Dharma, their [karmic retribution] shall be transformed."
If those who undergo the sufferings of hell can attain the Land of Peace and Bliss, this applies even more so to those with heavy offenses, let alone those with light offenses;
how much more so for those without offenses? It applies even to those without merit, let alone those with merit; how much more so for those with abundant merit?

It applies even to a single thought-moment, let alone many moments; how much more so for a year or a lifetime? Their rebirth in that land will certainly not be among the middle or lower grades. This has been the great tradition throughout antiquity and the present.

The various masters of the Dharma who manifest signs of rebirth in the Pure Land are all its proof. Now, the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation specifically accords with the capacities of beings throughout the ten directions;

it benefits all three grades of faculties equally, as the faculty of hearing is universally penetrating. The [practice of] the Ear-faculty’s Perfect Penetration specifically accords with the capacities of beings in this region;

it benefits only those of superior faculties. Furthermore, it was shown to Ānanda so that he might return home by way of the path; thus, the Great Being Mañjuśrī specifically selected it for him. It is not...
This means that while the faculty of hearing is preeminent, mindfulness of the Buddha is relatively inferior. Those who recite the scriptures should not fail to understand this.
That a practitioner of Chan has transcribed this sutra with their own blood to circulate the Great Dharma is truly a rare and extraordinary feat;
they will surely have a share in rebirth in the Pure Land.

Regarding the period of Buddha-recollection, there are accounts of those who have not yet perceived the marks and signs even after the passing of three weeks, and so forth.
Observing the intensity of their application of mind and the vigor of their practice, one may expect that within these hundred days, there will certainly be a great and inconceivable accomplishment.
However, at this time, one must not harbor a pre-conceived expectation of results; to harbor such a mind increases restlessness and, conversely, becomes an obstacle.

This is a subtle mental affliction within the gate of cultivation; it must not remain unknown. One must simply have deep faith and clear realization that there is no Buddha outside the mind and no mind outside the Buddha.
The entire mind is the Buddha, and the entire Buddha is the mind. When a single thought manifests before one, that is the correspondence of a single thought;
when every thought manifests before one, that is the correspondence of every thought. It is only necessary to ensure that this mindfulness is ever-present.
When this manifests before you, it is the true efficacy. To seek efficacy apart from this mindfulness is to create an interruption;
it is to lack intimacy; it is to enter upon a forked path. As the Sūtra says: "This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha."
This is precisely what is meant by that. My humble view is thus; I do not know what you, Layman, think of it.
As for Changshui’s question and Langya’s answer, they are as direct and clear as the point of a needle; it would be redundant to add anything further, like a "snake's foot.
If one can truly have this correct eye opened wide here, one will see through Langya and capture Changshui in defeat. The great purport of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*—[consider this].
It is already more than half finished. Nevertheless, even so, it would be better to cast it away into another world and simply focus one’s mind on the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
If one were to open a path for minor intellectual understanding, there would be no need to laboriously bring it forth at all.

As for the *Chazilu*, I have long heard of its reputation, but as I have not personally seen the text, I cannot yet pass judgment upon it. Recently, in this monastery, there has been only the lay practitioner Jiayuan.
I visit only once every ten days or so; apart from this, there are no other traces of guests. Day after day, I join with the various *śramaṇas* to brandish the fly-whisk and discuss the sutras.
When these sessions conclude, I burn incense and sit in tranquil meditation. Sometimes I collate the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and sometimes I examine the "ferry-crossings" and "beams" [of the teachings].

Aside from these, I have no other affairs. I have already finished lecturing on six fascicles of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*; I expect that by the seventh month of the coming year, the entire work will be completed.
Reflecting upon this, to have completed two recitations of this sutra within half a year is indeed a great joy for a person born in Jambudvīpa.
Nevertheless, it has been merely a matter of following the lines and tracing the ink; not a single new word has been gained. I record this to invite a laugh from my readers.
Reply to Layman Peng Er-lin of Jiangnan:

I respectfully observe that you, Layman, have deeply entered the Pure Land school and extensively bestowed the gift of Dharma, benefiting both yourself and others; your understanding and practice are both perfected.

One may truly say that you manifest in the body of a layperson (*gṛhapati*) while practicing the bodhisattva path, never deviating from your original vows and never forgetting your debt to the Buddha.
Previously, having obtained three new treatises on the sutras, I rashly composed critical evaluations of them; that I was not censured for this was already beyond my expectations.

Now, you have again sent me various newly carved works, entrusting me with the task of providing definitive commentaries upon them. This makes me feel all the more ashamed. As a mere mountain recluse, I possess nothing but the Great Vehicle of the Teachings (*śāsana*).
The essential meaning: I have a rough understanding of the general direction, yet having lost the opportunity for formal study since my youth, my speech does not form coherent compositions.
Consequently, during my twenty-odd years as abbot in two locations, I have never offered so much as a single word to the gates of patrons and protectors.

Now, moved by the layman’s open-mindedness in seeking me from afar and his sincerity in seeking the Dharma, I have suddenly cast aside my rustic ignorance and exhausted all that I know to report to you with direct words. Whether this is correct or not—[let it be judged].

I take this to heart; may you, O Illustrious One, decide for yourself. Both the *Nianfo jueyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts through Mindfulness of the Buddha) and the [other] treatise have brought forth insights never before revealed by predecessors.
The one demonstrates the transcendence of his wisdom and understanding, while the other manifests the sincerity of his defense of the Way.

Both are the extraordinary deeds of a great man of immeasurable capacity, worthy of being included in the Tripiṭaka for eternal circulation. The prefaces and postscripts are all refined and appropriate. In some instances...
There are points worthy of discussion, which I shall address in detail later.
Regarding the frequent letters sent by the lay practitioner Li Ruiyi, I have not yet replied to them.
Since our minds as teacher and disciple are in accord, you will surely not suspect me. I hear that you are currently in the south.
He labored diligently in public service and devoted his heart to protecting the Dharma. His practice was never interrupted, and his exhortations were most earnest.
Thus, he simultaneously accomplished the two benefits of self-cultivation and the transformation of others; worldly affairs and the Buddha-dharma proceeded as one path.

Whether through occasional correspondence or by word of mouth, whenever anyone heard or saw of it, they were both comforted and filled with joy. Reflecting on this, I consider that the Way is omnipresent; how could it be partitioned?

Whether among the clergy or the laity, there is indeed a difference between ease and difficulty at the time of cultivation and realization. To speak precisely of the path of practice, it is already not easy for those who have left the household life, let alone for those who remain at home.

Since it is difficult even for those living as householders, how much more so for those holding official positions? Therefore, one knows that the very dust and toil of worldly life can be made into the work of the Buddha.
To transform heat and affliction into coolness and clarity— if one were not one who has realized non-arising through patience,

attained the stage of non-retrogression, entered deeply into the chamber of the Tathāgata, and manifested the body of a civil official as a skillful means— then it would be feared that one could never avoid being gradually defiled by worldly conditions,

and one’s aspiration for the Way would diminish day by day. Now, you, my worthy friend, though you have not long since turned toward this Path, are already able, amidst the bustle and complexity of an official office, to exert yourself with fierce resolve.
It is truly so. Were it not for the power of roots of goodness cultivated in past lives, how could this be?

Nevertheless, one must still deeply reflect upon the lack of peace within the three realms, the suffering and affliction of the physical body, the perilous path of birth and death, and the impermanence of human life. It is fortunate that you have heard the Buddha-dharma and fortunately given rise to faith.
Break through illusory phenomena and illusory conditions with the single eye; shoulder the Buddha-mind and the Buddha-practice with naked integrity. This is pure karma.
Practice what you have attained and cultivate it further. When it is time to leave the field of official service, leave it immediately; do not harbor even the slightest lingering attachment.
Do not waste your precious time, but strive to accomplish your life's purpose so that you may bloom in the highest grade of rebirth.

In this way, you will not fail the virtuous vows cultivated through many lifetimes by yourself, nor the compassionate grace of our Buddha who has protected and mindful of you for long kalpas, thereby fulfilling your worldly and transcendental aspirations for this one lifetime.
