The One Sentence of Amitābha in the *Śatagāthā-śāstra*:
The essential heart-essence of our Buddha, Vertically penetrating the five periods [of the Buddha’s teaching], Horizontally encompassing the eight teachings.
What is the intent of this "One Sentence of Amitābha"? Those who truly know it are always few; Those who merely hear it are far more numerous.
A single phrase of Amitābha—its great meaning is clear. Like a snake appearing in the reflection of a bow, or medicine emerging from a golden flask.
A single phrase of Amitābha is a skillful means of diverse names; it universally gathers all capacities and provides a secondary thread of access.
A single phrase of Amitābha opens the gate of rebirth; this is a source of vast merit, not a minor root of goodness.
One phrase of Amitābha: at the moment of death, the Buddha appears; the four analytical powers are personally proclaimed, and the six directions join in praise.
One phrase of Amitābha: the standard for attaining Buddhahood; with a mind of mindfulness, one enters the patience of non-arising.
One phrase of Amitābha: realizing the three stages of non-retrogression; in this single lifetime alone, one spreads out the seat of Buddhahood.
One phrase of Amitābha fulfills the ten great vows; how could it be that Samantabhadra taught it in vain?
To practice one phrase of Amitābha is like a white ox pulling with vigor, swift as the wind, its gait level and upright.
One phrase of Amitābha is the Tathāgatagarbha mind: beyond the water there are no waves; the vessel was originally gold.
A single phrase of Amitābha is the wondrous nature of True Suchness; Spring resides within the flowering branches, and the image is contained within the ancient mirror.
A single phrase of Amitābha is the pure and real mark; Beyond discussion and beyond thought, it is difficult to name and difficult to describe.
A single phrase of Amitābha is the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm; Manifesting its entire essence as the absolute truth, its interpenetration is without obstruction.
One phrase of Amitābha: The great, perfect mirror of wisdom, Body and land reflected within, Layer upon layer, mutually illuminating.
One phrase of Amitābha: The empty Tathāgatagarbha, Before the myriad dharmas had taken form, The single truth is beyond all marks.
One phrase of Amitābha: Perfect Bodhi, Heaven has nothing higher; The clouds cannot equal it.
One phrase of Amitābha; The Great Parinirvāṇa. A single orb of bright moon; Ten thousand *li* of empty cold.

One who has life must inevitably face death (under heaven, from antiquity to the present, not a single person has ever escaped it).

Second, believe that human life is impermanent (though the outgoing breath may remain, the incoming breath is difficult to preserve; if even one breath does not return, one has entered the next world).

Third, believe that the cycle of rebirth is a perilous path (a single moment’s lapse leads to falling into the evil realms; obtaining a human body is like the soil on a fingernail, while losing it is like the soil of the great earth).
Fourth, believing that the duration of the miserable realms is long (a single retribution in the three paths lasts five thousand kalpas; how much longer will it be when one emerges from them again?).
Fifth, believing that the Buddha’s words are not false (these sun and moon orbs may fall, and Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, may be shaken, but what the Buddhas say is never otherwise).
Sixth, believe that the Pure Land truly exists (just as this Sahā world does now; it is vividly and presently real).

Seventh, believe that by making the vow to be born there, one will indeed be born there (if you now make the vow, you shall be born there now; the sutras have clear evidence of this—how could they deceive me?).
The eighth stage, the Stage of Faith, is non-retrogressive (because the objects are supreme and conditions are powerful, the mind of retrogression does not arise).
The ninth stage, the Stage of Faith, achieves Buddhahood in one lifetime (with immeasurable lifespan, what task could not be accomplished?).

The Dharma-source of the Ten Faiths is Mind-Only (Mind-Only possesses both the meanings of "endowment" and "creation"; as with all dharmas mentioned above, they are all endowed within my mind and all created by my mind).
Because one believes the Buddha’s words, one performs the latter four practices; because one does not believe the Buddha’s words, one performs only the former four.
Therefore, to have deep faith in the Buddha’s words is to have deep faith in one's own mind.

For those who cultivate the practice of purity and can possess these ten kinds of faith, birth in that Land of Bliss is like taking a left-hand promissory note to retrieve a previously deposited object—how could it be difficult?

A Brief Account of the Conduct of Chan Master Chewu.
His name was Ji-xing; his courtesy name was Chewu; he was also styled Netang and titled Mengdong. He was from Fengrun County, Shandong.
His secular surname was Ma; his father’s name was Wan-zhang, and his mother was of the Gao clan. From childhood, the Master was exceptionally gifted;

as he grew up, he delighted in reading, and there were none among the classics, histories, or various other texts that he did not examine and study. At the age of twenty-two, due to a severe illness, he realized the illusory nature and impermanence of the physical body.
Having developed a transcendent resolve, his illness was cured. He traveled to Fangshan County and received the tonsure under the veteran monk Rongchi at Sansheng An.
The following year, he went to Xiuyun Temple to receive full ordination from Vinaya Master Hengshi.

The next year, hearing that Dharma Master Longyi of Xiangjie Temple was expounding the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Master attended the assembly. Morning and night he engaged in inquiry and debate, seeking the profound meanings with great diligence. Thus...

He fully realized the essential meaning of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*). Furthermore, he relied upon Master Huì'àn of Zēngshòu Temple to lecture on the *Abhidharma* school (*xiāngzōng*), attaining its profound essentials.
Later, he attended Master Biànkōng at Xīnhuá Temple, where he heard the *Lotus*, *Śūraṅgama*, and *Vajra* sūtras.

His perfect understanding suddenly opened up regarding the principles of the two schools of Nature and Characteristics (*xìngxiāng*) and the three contemplations and ten stages (*sānguān shíshèng*). He attained complete realization.
He was free from all obstructions. In the winter of the thirty-third year of the Qianlong era, he visited Guangtong Chuiru Chun’ung to investigate the matter of the ultimate direction.

As teacher and disciple found their paths in perfect accord, Chun’ung certified his realization of the mind. He thus became the thirty-sixth generation successor of Linji and the seventh generation successor of Qing Shan.
In the thirty-eighth year, when Chun’ung moved to Wanshou Temple, the Master succeeded him at Guangtong and led the assembly in practice.

Regarding Chan, he exhorted and encouraged his junior disciples tirelessly, as if every year were but a single day. His reputation spread throughout the north and south, and the style of his school flourished greatly.

Whenever he recalled Master Yongming Yanshou, a master craftsman of the Chan gate who still turned his heart toward the Pure Land and daily recited the name of Amitābha Buddha one hundred thousand times, vowing to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), he felt that in this present degenerate age, it was especially fitting to follow and uphold his example. Thereupon—
He settled his mind upon the Pure Land and championed the Lotus School (*Lianzong*). He limited his daily reception of guests to the duration of a single stick of incense;
beyond that, he engaged in nothing but prostrations and the recitation of mantras. In the fifty-seventh year [of his life], he moved to Juesheng Temple, where he served as abbot for eight years.

There, he restored all neglected matters and established three additional halls outside the Jingye Hall (Hall of Pure Practice), naming them Nirvana, Anxiang (Pure Abode), and Xueshi (Scholar). This was intended to accommodate the elderly and the infirm.

Those who sought his guidance found a place of reliance. Beginners found it convenient for their recitation and practice. As for the fundamental principles of Chan and Pure Land, the Master had deeply penetrated their mysteries.

He was extremely strict in disciplining himself and very earnest in his expectations of others. When he provided instruction and preached the Dharma, it flowed like water poured from a vessel or arose like clouds gathering in the sky.

Together with the assembly, he cultivated his practice with diligence. Like a great wind fanning the lotus, his transformative influence was venerated from afar and near; both monastics and laypeople turned their hearts toward him.

At that time, he was considered the foremost figure within the Dharma-gate. In the fifth year of the Jiaping era, he retired to Zifu Temple on Mount Hongluo, intending to spend the remainder of his life there.
The patch-robed disciples who followed him out of devotion were numerous. For the sake of the Dharma and for the sake of people, the Master’s heart never grew weary;

he thus remained to stay with the assembly once more. Before long, it became a monastic center. Carrying firewood, drawing water, plastering walls, and repairing roofs—down to every drink and every meal—he shared these things with the community.
He continued in this manner for another ten years. In the second month of the fifteenth year, he went to Wanshou Temple to sweep the grave of his ancestor, Master Cui.
He took leave of his mountain patrons, saying: "Illusory conditions do not endure; human life is impermanent. A life lived in vain is to be lamented; each of you should strive to practice *nien-fo*.
In years to come, we shall meet again well in the Pure Land. In the third month, he returned to the mountain and ordered that preparations for the cremation be made in advance.
On the seventeenth day of the tenth month, he gathered the assembly to hand over the affairs of the monastery and instructed his disciple Songquan to take charge.
The assembly of abbots was admonished as follows: "The Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation universally benefits those of the three capacities and leaves no one without its reach.

For many years, I have worked with great diligence alongside you all to establish this monastery; my original purpose was to welcome visitors from afar so that we might together cultivate the Pure Land practice.
You must forever observe the regulations I have established and must not change the fundamental direction or alter the course. Only thus shall you not bring shame upon this old monk."

This was a shared expression of sincere resolve among the assembly. Half a month before his passing, he felt a slight ailment in his body and instructed the congregation to join him in chanting the Buddha’s name.
Suddenly, he saw countless banners and streamers appearing in the void, coming from the west. He then addressed the assembly, saying:
The signs of the Pure Land appeared, and he said, "I am about to return to the West. The assembly urged him to remain in the world, but the Master replied, "A hundred years are but a sojourn;
in the end, one must have a place of return. That I may attain the sacred realm is your good fortune as disciples; why do you distress yourselves by urging me to stay?"
On the sixteenth day of the twelfth month, he instructed Master Guanyi, the head of the monastery, to prepare a Nirvana feast.
At the hour of Shen on the seventeenth day, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Yesterday I already beheld the three great bodhisattvas—Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
today I have further received the Buddha’s personal guidance and escort. I am now departing. The assembly recited the Buddha’s name with ever-increasing fervor as the Master sat upright, facing west.
With palms joined, she uttered the Great Name once and beheld a portion of the Buddha’s marks and signs. She then formed the Maitreya Seal (*Mithila-mudrā*) and passed away with serene composure.
The assembly heard a wondrous fragrance wafting through the air. Her remains were enshrined for seven days; her countenance remained as if alive, her expression compassionate, harmonious, and full.
Her white hair turned black, and its luster was extraordinary. On the second week, she was placed in the coffin; on the third week, she was cremated, and śarīra relics were obtained.
There were over one hundred grains [of relics]. His disciples, following his final instructions, requested that his remains be interred within the Universal Stupa (Pútóngtǎ).

The Master was born on the fourteenth day of the tenth month in the sixth year of the Qianlong era at the hour of Wei; he passed away on the seventeenth day of the twelfth month in the fifteenth year of the Jiaqing era at the hour of Shen.
He reached a secular age of seventy and a monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera-vassa*) of forty-nine, with a dharma seniority (*dharma-vassa*) of forty.

There were three [works]. He left behind the *Shi Chanjiao lu ni fo jietuo xing* (Verses on the Practice of Reciting the Buddha’s Name within the Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya), which circulated in the world.

On the full moon of the ninth month in the seventeenth year of the Jiaqing era (the Ren-shen year), a disciple of the Master named Xingcong brought the Master’s biography and requested that I compose a preface.
I have been in accord with the Master for many years and have long received his instruction, from which I have gained much enlightenment. The Master was truly...

He was a man of extraordinary capacity. His six sense-faculties were keen and penetrating, and his realization transcended the ordinary. Possessing eloquence, he simultaneously maintained ascetic practices with consistency from beginning to end.
As I have witnessed this with my own eyes, I have recorded it here without a single word of embellishment.
I regret my lack of literary skill, yet I have sought to express the truth specifically so as to transmit this account with credibility. Written by Duṭuo Tikuantong of Nianhua Monastery.
